_note: Per-feature standing against Unity / Unreal / Godot, one row per capability, WITH EVIDENCE.  The 2026-08-31 audit compared 342 features and published an aggregate -- 51 ahead / 112 parity / 145 behind / 30 absent / 4 n/a -- and then the rows were gone: only the totals survived, in a report. A measurement whose evidence is not stored cannot be re-run, so the split could not move as work landed, and a split that cannot move is a number that quietly stops being true. This file is that measurement made re-runnable. Every row carries `evidence`: a file:line, a command, or the landed item that changed it. tools/report_parity.py computes the split; tools/lint/check_parity_ledger.py fails on a row with no evidence, an unknown status, or a duplicate id.

_status_values.ahead: JCE does this and the compared engines do not, or do it less well.
_status_values.parity: equivalent in practice for a shipping game.
_status_values.behind: present but weaker, or present and not reachable from where it matters.
_status_values.na: does not apply to this engine's shape.

audit_day._note: The published aggregate, kept as the historical baseline. The rows behind it were not stored, which is why `rows` here (342) is larger than the number of entries in `features` below: this ledger holds only what has been RE-measured with evidence since. The gap is stated rather than hidden -- report_parity.py prints both.

features.feature: Blendshape deformation runs on the GPU, not the CPU
features.evidence: BUILT 2026-09-17, and the row moves because the headline claim is now true: the deform runs on the GPU. cs_morph_deform.sc is one compute dispatch per morph-bearing primitive, one thread per vertex, reading device-resident base vertices and TARGET-MAJOR deltas that every instance of the model SHARES and writing the dynamic vertex buffer the colour pass draws (jce_morph_gpu.c). That sharing is the point: the CPU path it replaces kept a FULL per-instance copy of the vertex array and rewrote it on the main thread every time a weight moved -- per instance, per frame, for a face rig that changes weights every frame by definition, on an engine whose stated baseline is one core. A weight change now costs one dispatch and four floats of uniform. || THE CPU PATH IS NOT DELETED, it is the fallback, gated on BGFX_CAPS_COMPUTE: compute needs GL 4.3 / ES 3.1 and this engine's desktop GL profile is 120 by design. So the two evaluators must agree, and cs_morph_deform.sc is written against jce_morph_apply line for line -- including that a normal is renormalised ONLY when the data carries normal deltas. || THE DISPATCH RUNS BEFORE THE DRAW, which took a view id below every scene base (JCE_VIEW_MORPH_DEFORM = 1, recorded in contracts/view-reservations.txt). bgfx executes views in ascending id order, so any id above a base would have executed AFTER the draw that reads its output and the mesh would have been one frame behind its own animation. || MEASURED, D3D11, 1280x856 viewport region. The fixture had to be AUTHORED: this tree had import, a CPU evaluator, an inspector, a scene component and a renderer path for blendshapes and ZERO .glb anywhere in it carrying a `targets` array, so the feature had never been rendered at all. tools/gen_morph_probe_glb.py emits a skinned quad with one target that shears its top edge; two scenes differ in one field. NOISE FLOOR (same build, same config, twice): 0 px -- not one pixel. CONTROL (weight 1 vs weight 0): 96,364 px changed (8.795%), max 33 -- the deform does something. EQUIVALENCE (GPU vs CPU evaluator, JCE_MORPH_CPU=1 as the ablation, confirmed by the absence of every morph_gpu log line): 10 px differ at max 1/255 out of 1.1M -- float summation order, not a disagreement. || THE FIRST CONTROL FAILED AND THAT IS WHY THERE IS ONE. The initial camera framed an empty grid: the quad is back-face culled from that side and drew nothing, so weight 1 and weight 0 were identical and the equivalence read 'below the noise floor' on two pictures of no subject. A reference cube placed beside it in the same frame separated 'the mesh did not draw' from 'the camera is not looking at it' in one capture. || THREE CEILINGS REMAIN, unchanged by this and each its own work: JCE_MORPH_MAX_WEIGHTS is 16; there are no TANGENT deltas (only POSITION and NORMAL morph); and the resolve loop is still gated on the entity having a SkeletalAnimator, so a static prop with blendshapes and no skeleton still cannot morph.
features.compared: Unity does blendshapes in the skinning compute/vertex path with no practical per-mesh target cap and morphs tangents. UE evaluates morph targets on the GPU (vertex-buffer deltas or a compute pass) and supports morph targets on static-ish skeletal meshes without an animator asset. Godot 4 has GPU blend shapes on MeshInstance3D including on non-skinned meshes. JCE's 16-weight cap, missing tangent deltas, full-vertex CPU copy per dirty frame, and skeletal-animator gate are all below that.

features.feature: Animator override controller
features.evidence: landed #178. The loader took a path and discarded it, so every caller's `if (!asset)` passed and the result was a permanent no-op -- the one outcome that cannot be told apart from working. It now parses {"pairs":[{original,override}]} and REFUSES every input that would substitute nothing (missing file, bad JSON, no 'pairs' key, empty array, half-written pairs), because an empty controller returned as a valid object is that same indistinguishable no-op with a file behind it. jce_sr_anim.c resolves through it at the two clip resolvers and the blend-tree match, so the state machine keeps its states, transitions and conditions and only the clip each state ASKS FOR is answered differently. THIS ROW'S OLD EVIDENCE WAS WRONG ON ITS PREMISE: it blamed jce_avatar_load being a stub, but an override controller substitutes clips in the CONTROLLER, not bones in a rig -- the avatar loader is not on this path at all. The inspector's unwired badge came off in the same commit; it was costing the player real bytes, since 'overrideController' was already an asset-dependency key in jce_bundle_deps.c and the packer cooked the file into the shipped PAK for a feature that did nothing. 6 new unit cases, 441/441.

features.feature: Humanoid rig / avatar retargeting
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-07. A humanoid bone vocabulary (22 roles -- the set Unity marks REQUIRED), auto-mapping from joint names, proportion-independent rotation retargeting, and the .avatar asset that carries a mapping.
jce_avatar_load NO LONGER RETURNS NULL FOR EVERYTHING: it reads a real .avatar (JSON, joint NAMES not indices -- an index means nothing outside the skeleton it was taken from, and re-exporting a model with one more bone shifts every one of them). It still answers NULL for a missing or unparseable file, which is what keeps that branch meaning 'there is no such file' rather than 'your rig has no bones'.
THE MATCHER IS TESTED AGAINST THE FOUR RIGGED MODELS ACTUALLY IN THIS TREE, which use three different conventions: Unreal (`pelvis`, `spine_02`, `upperarm_l`, `calf_r`, `ball_l`), Blender (`HIP CONTROLLER`, `UPPER ARM.L`, `SHIN.R`) and the Khronos samples (`torso_joint_2`, `arm_joint_L_3`, `Skeleton_neck_joint_2`). Names invented for a test would have passed and then met a real rig.
IT CAUGHT A REAL AMBIGUITY: PSX_BagMan has `HIP CONTROLLER` for the hips AND `HIP.L` / `HIP.R` for the leg roots. An unsided rule now REFUSES a name that carries a side, so the left hip cannot claim JCE_HB_HIPS; before that, which one won came down to which joint the file happened to list first.
RETARGETING, tested on two skeletons that agree about nothing -- different names, joint counts, order, rest poses and SIZE:
  a 50-degree rotation on the source's upper arm arrives as 50 degrees from the TARGET's own rest pose (within 1 degree), not as the source's absolute orientation -- which would have dragged the source's 20-degree rest rotation across and fought the target's -35.
  NEGATIVE CONTROL: retargeting the source's REST pose moves no target joint by more than 0.5 degrees. Without it, a retarget that merely COPIED rotations would pass the test above whenever the two rest poses happened to be close.
  a joint no role names keeps its rest pose exactly; an IK helper (`TARGET.L`) is not mapped.
  root translation is scaled by the hips-height ratio: a 1 m stride onto a rig of half the height arrives as 0.5 m -- the same stride RELATIVE TO THE BODY.
  the avatar round-trips through save/load and binds BY NAME: bound to the rig it came from it resolves; bound to the other rig it resolves NOTHING rather than pointing at whatever now occupies index 3.
A DEFECT THIS FOUND IN THE SKELETON API'S TWO REST SOURCES: the hips height was read from jce_skeleton_rest_pose() while the rotations came from jce_skeleton_rest_trs(). A skeleton built with rest_translation set and local_transform left identity -- which the API permits -- gave a height of 0 through one and the right answer through the other. It now reads the TRS, which jce_skeleton.h itself calls the original glTF node values.
EDITOR: the Animation Rigging panel gained a Humanoid section -- Unity's Configure Avatar -- listing every role and the joint that plays it. It prefers the SAVED .avatar over auto-detection when one exists, and colours a role whose stored joint name is not in the rig, which is the one case the panel exists to make visible: a broken avatar that a detector would paper over with a working-looking mapping the runtime will not use.
WHY 'behind' AND NOT 'parity': the runtime does not retarget yet. JceSkeletalAnimator still plays a clip on the skeleton it was authored for; nothing calls jce_humanoid_retarget per frame, so a clip from rig A does not yet play on rig B by itself -- the transport exists and the wiring does not. And there is no IK, no muscle-space clamping and no per-bone twist redistribution; Unity's Humanoid has all three and they are the difference between 'the motion transfers' and 'the hands land where the animator put them'. Both limits are stated in jce_humanoid.h rather than left to be found.
2026-09-08 -- THE PER-FRAME CALLER LANDED, and the row's own claim needed one correction on the way. It said 'the runtime does not retarget yet'. The runtime DOES retarget, and has: sr_anim_try_retarget resolves the source model, samples the clip against the source rig and transfers the pose -- BY JOINT NAME (jce_anim_retarget.h). What was true is the narrower and more interesting statement: nothing called the ROLE-based retarget, and a name map covers rigs that share a naming convention and NOTHING else. Two humanoid rigs from different tools share no bone names at all, so the name map matches zero joints, every bone falls back to the destination rest pose, and the clip visibly does nothing. That is exactly the case Unity's Humanoid exists for.
BOTH MAPS ARE NOW BUILT AND THE ONE THAT COVERS MORE JOINTS IS USED. A TIE GOES TO THE NAME MAP, so every rig pair that matched by name before takes exactly the path it took and produces exactly the pose it produced -- a fixed threshold would have been a number with no reason behind it, and would have moved existing content the day it was picked wrong. The choice is logged when the roles win, because 'my clip suddenly works' deserves an explanation in the log as much as 'my clip does nothing' did.
The role path decomposes to local ROTATIONS either side of the transfer, because that is the form jce_humanoid_retarget speaks and keeping the matrix layout out of it keeps that function about the transfer. The destination's translation and scale stay its own -- limb lengths belong to the target rig -- and only the hips' translation crosses, scaled by the two rigs' hips heights.
TESTED AT THE POINT WHERE THE DECISION IS DECIDABLE WITHOUT A RENDERER: for the two differently-named rigs the existing fixture already builds, the role map covers STRICTLY MORE than the name map, and at least three roles -- the second assertion so the test fails if the fixture ever stops exercising what it was built for rather than silently comparing zero against zero.
jce_sr_anim.c crossed the 3000-line cap when this landed, so retarget playback moved to jce_sr_anim_retarget.c -- the same answer jce_ui_canvas.c got twice, and for the same reason: raising the cap is cheaper and wrong. The seam is seven values and no frame struct.
STILL NOT CLAIMED, and unchanged from before: no IK, no muscle-space clamping and no per-bone twist redistribution. Unity's Humanoid has all three and they are the difference between 'the motion transfers' and 'the hands land where the animator put them'. Both limits stay stated in jce_humanoid.h rather than left to be found. || 2026-09-17 -- MUSCLE-SPACE CLAMPING LANDED, one of the three named gaps closed and the other two unchanged. The transfer was unbounded by construction: it carries the rotation the animation ADDED, so a source rig whose shin the animator rolled 120 degrees about its own length hands the target 120 degrees, and nothing in the transfer knows a knee has a front. That is not a hypothetical -- it is what crossing two tools' bone-roll conventions produces, which is the case the role map exists for. LIMITS ARE ON THE DELTA, NOT THE POSE: 'how far may an animation push this bone from its own rest' is rig-independent; 'where may this bone point' is not, because it depends on how the artist built the rest pose. Decomposed swing/twist about the bone's OWN axis, and the axis comes from the RIG (the rest direction from the joint playing a role to the joint playing the role below it) rather than from a convention -- this tree already carries Unreal, Blender and Khronos-sample conventions in four models, and 'which local axis runs down the bone' is a different answer in each. A role with no derivable axis (a tip; a role whose child is missing from the rig) is LEFT ALONE rather than clamped about a guess. APPEND-ONLY: jce_humanoid_retarget is byte-identical to what it was and delegates with clamping off, so existing content animates exactly as before; jce_humanoid_retarget_clamped is the new entry point and the runtime path passes true. The clamp returns the caller's own bits when the delta is already in range -- exactly, not approximately -- so a pose that needed no clamping is not quietly re-quantised every frame and a test asking 'did it fire' has an exact answer. TESTED IN PAIRS, because a clamp that fires on everything is as wrong as one that fires on nothing and only the second looks like a bug: 8 cases -- the axis points down the bone and is unit length; a tip returns false; a delta inside the range comes back bit-for-bit; 120 deg of twist lands on the knee's 30 and -120 on its -30; 150 deg of swing lands on the 80 deg cone; the per-role numbers actually differ (shoulder tighter than upper arm); and through the RETARGET, clamp on vs off -- 120 deg in gives 120 off and 30 on with one role reported clamped, while 20 deg in gives BIT-IDENTICAL output and zero roles clamped. EDITOR: the Animation Rigging panel's Humanoid section gained a Muscle range column beside the joint that plays each role -- Unity's Muscles & Settings, and it is on that row rather than its own tab because a limit shown away from the joint it binds is a number nobody can check. A role with no derivable axis says so instead of showing limits it will never be held to. 15 locales. STILL NOT CLAIMED: no IK after the retarget, and no per-bone twist redistribution. And the clamp is a CONE plus a signed twist, which cannot say 'a knee bends forward and not back' -- that needs a hinge AXIS, and a hinge axis is not derivable from a rest pose where the leg is straight (the cross product of two collinear bones is zero). Unity gets it from a configured T-pose; until this engine has that configuration step, hinge DIRECTION is unclamped and jce_humanoid.h says so rather than letting a reader assume otherwise. || 2026-09-18 -- TWO-BONE IK LANDED, the first of the three gaps this row names, and the other two are unchanged. jce_humanoid_ik_two_bone puts a limb's end effector on a model-space target by the law of cosines -- analytic, so there is no iteration count to tune and no convergence to fail; CCD and FABRIK earn their keep on longer chains and on three joints would only add a knob. WHY IT IS NEEDED AT ALL is the retarget's own design: it transfers ROTATIONS, which is right because limb lengths belong to the target rig, and the cost is that identical shoulder and elbow angles put the hand elsewhere on a rig with a longer forearm -- so a clip authored with a hand on a railing has it through the railing. Unity corrects that with Humanoid IK goals, UE with a Two Bone IK node. TESTED IN PAIRS, because an IK solver fails quietly in two directions and only one of them looks wrong: it can MISS (and 'close enough' passes a visual check) and it can move joints it was not asked to move (a shoulder that drifts whenever a hand is pinned, found three weeks later). 9 cases: the hand lands to 1e-4 on a rig whose bones are 0.5; it lands on NINE directions around the shoulder, not just the plane it was debugged in; an unreachable target points the limb straight at it rather than refusing (refusing leaves the pose untouched and reads as 'the IK never ran'); pelvis, spine and the hand itself come back BIT-FOR-BIT while the upper and lower provably changed, so the test cannot pass by the solver doing nothing; weight 0 is bit-for-bit AND returns true, because false would make 'the blend is at zero' read as 'this rig has no arm'; a partial weight lands STRICTLY between the two poses, which fails if it silently behaves as either endpoint; and two opposite pole hints put the elbow >0.1 apart while both still reach to 1e-4. TWO REAL DEFECTS THE TESTS CAUGHT, both in the degenerate case a rest pose hits every time: (1) a straight limb has no bend plane of its own, and the first fallback took an axis perpendicular to the TARGET direction alone -- which came out PARALLEL to the limb for an arm hanging -Y with the target straight out +X, and rotating a bone about its own length does not bend it. One direction of eight missed by 0.25 of a 1.0 reach. The plane has to contain the limb. (2) folding the pole hint into that same axis reached only the limbs that were ALREADY bent, so on a rest pose two opposite poles produced the same elbow; the pole is now an explicit roll about the A->target line after the aim, where 'which side is the elbow on' is asked and answered instead of being encoded in the sign of a cross product. STILL BEHIND, and for a named reason: the solver has NO CALLER. Its consumer is a goal, and in Unity a goal is a scripting call (Animator.SetIKPosition inside OnAnimatorIK), not an inspector control. Exposing it to scripts means appending to JceScriptHost -- byte-append-only ABI -- plus the seven-language regeneration, which is its own change; it is recorded in tools/lint/editor_consumption_exempt.txt rather than left to be discovered. Per-bone twist redistribution and hinge DIRECTION (which needs a configured T-pose, since the cross product of two collinear bones is zero on a straight leg) are also unchanged, and jce_humanoid.h says so rather than letting a reader assume otherwise. || 2026-09-19 -- THE GOAL HAS AN AUTHORING SURFACE, so the second of this row's three named gaps is closed and the row stays behind for the other two. JceIkConstraint gains kind 7, HumanoidLimb: root_bone names a LIMB ("LeftArm", "RightArm", "LeftLeg", "RightLeg") and the three joints come from the rig's JceHumanoidMap instead of from three authored bone names. That is the difference Unity's AvatarIKGoal exists for and a named triple cannot express: two humanoid rigs from different tools share no bone names, so a goal authored against one covers nothing on the other. IT IS A KIND, NOT A SECOND SYSTEM. The engine already had a wired constraint pass -- sr_apply_ik_constraints, called from sr_update_skinned_anims, solving seven kinds -- so kind 7 changes exactly one thing: WHERE the three joint indices come from. The solve, the weight, the pole and the rotation write-back are the kind-1 path unchanged. No ABI append, no new component field, no new serialization key: which field means what is already kind-dependent in that struct (kinds 2/3/4 read root_bone and target_entity and nothing else). MEASURED END TO END on PSX_BagMan, the Blender-convention rig this row's matcher was originally tested against (UPPER ARM.L / FOREARM.L / HAND.L). Two scene files differing in EXACTLY ONE LINE -- "enabled": false vs true on the constraint, verified by diff before the comparison was allowed -- moved 23623 px (2.156%) of the viewport against a NOISE FLOOR OF 0 px, peak 223. The left arm raises and its hand goes to the target cube; the right arm, torso, legs and head are unchanged. THE FIRST FIXTURE WAS UNUSABLE AND SAID SO: with the clip playing, the noise floor was 72620 px (6.6% of the viewport) because the pose is a function of wall time and two captures are two processes -- larger than anything an IK goal on one arm could produce. Freezing the animator took it to 0. UNIT: tests/renderer/... no -- tests/middleware/animation/test_jce_humanoid_limb_goal.c walks the same two steps the renderer does (limb -> roles -> map.joint[]) and requires the result to be the SAME joints a correct kind-1 triple would have named, that left and right do not resolve to each other, and that the triple is a parent chain (the analytic solver assumes it, and a non-chain triple would produce a pose with no error anywhere). EDITOR: the Animation Rigging panel's kind combo gains it, and on that kind the three bone boxes are REPLACED by one limb picker -- leaving them visible would show three controls the solver does not read, and a control that does nothing costs the reader more than no control. 15 locales, written per language. AND ONE MORE THING THIS DID NOT DO, said plainly because it would otherwise read as done: jce_humanoid_ik_two_bone -- the solver added on 2026-09-18 -- STILL HAS NO CALLER. Kind 7 routes through the renderer's existing jce_anim_ik_two_bone_solve, which works on model-space joint positions and writes rotations back into the skin palette; the humanoid solver works on a local-rotation pose, which is the shape the RETARGET holds. That is its natural caller -- 'a clip authored with a hand on a railing has it through the railing' is a retarget artefact -- and wiring it there is a separate change. || 2026-09-20 -- EFFECTOR PRESERVATION LANDED, which gives jce_humanoid_ik_two_bone the caller the entry above said it still lacked, and the measuring found TWO REAL DEFECTS ON THE WAY -- one of them already shipping. JceSkeletalAnimatorComponent.retarget_effector_ik (default OFF, Unity's IK Pass): after the role transfer and after the muscle clamp, each limb's end effector is IK'd back to where the SOURCE rig put it, expressed in the source hips' posed frame, scaled by the two rigs' hips heights, and re-expressed in the destination hips' frame. The number scales the ROOT TRANSLATION on every role retarget, so a 1 m stride onto it arrived as 206 m. The existing test could not see it: both of its fixture rigs are Y-up, and a defect in an axis assumption cannot be found by a fixture that shares the assumption. It is now the hips-to-feet DISTANCE -- axis-free, and also the quantity a stride actually scales with. Y-up content does not move (all 22 animation/retarget tests unchanged); what moves is the rigs it was silently wrong about. BOTH ARMS move from sticking out to hanging at the sides, which is where the source's walk puts them; BOTH LEGS are untouched, because the chain guard refuses BagMan's control-bone feet. THREE MEASUREMENTS WERE WRONG BEFORE THIS ONE WAS RIGHT, and each was caught by looking rather than by a number: (1) zero pixels changed, because hips_height was 5 mm and the targets landed 40 m away, unreachable, so the solver just aimed the limbs; (2) 13.97% changed and the POSE WAS BROKEN -- legs folded up, feet detached -- because the offset was copied raw between a Z-up and a Y-up rig, so 'above the hips' became 'in front of'; (3) 14.39% with the frame fixed, still with detached feet, which is what sent the search to the control bone. STILL BEHIND: per-bone twist redistribution, and hinge DIRECTION (which needs a configured T-pose, since the cross product of two collinear bones is zero on a straight leg). || 2026-09-20 -- PER-BONE TWIST REDISTRIBUTION LANDED, the second of the three gaps this row named, leaving one. jce_humanoid_redistribute_twist moves a fraction of the wrist's and ankle's twist onto the forearm and shin -- Unity's Fore Arm / Leg Twist -- wired to JceSkeletalAnimatorComponent.retarget_twist (0..1, default 0) and run BEFORE the effector IK, because the IK overwrites the upper and lower rotations outright and afterwards the redistribution would be discarded on exactly the limbs the IK touched. STILL BEHIND, and now down to ONE named gap: hinge DIRECTION. Unity gets it from a configured T-pose. Until this engine has that configuration step the row stays behind, and jce_humanoid.h says so rather than letting a reader assume otherwise. || 2026-09-20 -- HINGE DIRECTION LANDED, the LAST of the three gaps this row has been naming since 2026-09-07, AND THE BLOCKER RECORDED AGAINST IT WAS WRONG. Every earlier entry said a hinge axis 'is not derivable from a rest pose where the leg is straight, since the cross product of two collinear bones is zero', and concluded that it needed a configured T-pose. True of the two BONES; false of the pair that actually answers it. A knee's hinge axis is the body's LATERAL axis, which comes from the two HIPS -- never collinear on a humanoid -- with up from the hips to the highest mapped spine role, falling back to the two shoulders when the legs are unmapped. Every input is a difference between two joints the rig itself nominated for a role: nothing is authored, no axis convention is assumed, and no configuration step is needed. WHICH SIGN IS LEGAL is closed form too: rotating by +theta displaces the ankle along cross(axis, ankle - knee) to first order, so the sign of that displacement along forward says whether +theta sends the foot forward. A knee sends it back. jce_humanoid_clamp_knee_direction runs inside the retarget right after the muscle clamp, in the same space and on the same delta, with 5 degrees of hyperextension allowed because real knees have some and a clamp that fires at exactly zero trips on poses an animator meant. Measured: a delta bending the knee 40 degrees BACKWARDS comes back at -5.0; a delta bending it 60 degrees the right way comes back as the caller's own BITS. KNEES ONLY, and said in the header rather than left to be found: an elbow's hinge axis is not the body's lateral axis -- it depends on how the rig rolls the upper arm, which differs per tool -- so guessing it would clamp correct animation. 4 of 4 mutations red: the legal direction inverted, a legal bend recomposed instead of returned, the knee-only restriction removed, and an underivable frame replaced by a guess. THAT LAST ONE PASSED THE FIRST VERSION OF ITS TEST, which used a single arbitrary delta that happened to be legal under the guessed frame; it now tries a 60-degree bend about each of six signed axes, which cannot all be legal under any frame. AND THE FIXTURE ITSELF WAS WRONG FIRST: its joints set rest_translation and left local_transform identity, which the API permits and which makes jce_skeleton_rest_pose() and jce_skeleton_rest_trs() answer differently about the same rig -- the exact shape of a defect this tree has already paid for once. A fixture inconsistent with itself cannot judge code that reads either; it now builds local_transform from the TRS.

2026-09-20 -- PARITY. The elbow was the last of the named gaps, and it closed differently from the knee, which is the point.

A KNEE'S HINGE AXIS COMES FROM THE BODY; AN ELBOW'S CANNOT. The two hips are never collinear, so a straight leg still yields a lateral axis. Which way a forearm flexes depends on how the rig ROLLS the upper arm, and that differs per tool -- so the only rig-intrinsic source is the plane the arm is ALREADY BENT IN at rest, which is exactly why riggers leave a bend. MEASURED on the two rigged humans in this tree: CesiumMan's arm rests at 147 degrees and gives a plane; PSX_BagMan's rests at EXACTLY 180 and does not. Below 5 degrees of rest bend jce_humanoid_hinge_axis REFUSES rather than guessing, and the Animation Rigging panel's new Hinge column is where a rigger sees which of their rigs can be protected -- an elbow clamped about an invented axis rejects correct animation, which is strictly worse than not clamping.

ONE DERIVATION, PUBLIC, BECAUSE THE SECOND ONE DISAGREED. The clamp's first test re-derived the axis itself and read jce_skeleton_rest_pose() -- which returns LOCAL matrices, as its docstring says -- as though it were model space. On the bent-arm fixture that turned an axis of (-1,0,0) into (-0.925,0.370,-0.084), 22 degrees out, and a correct clamp came back as -15.7 degrees where -5 was asked. The red was about the test. jce_humanoid_hinge_axis is now the single derivation, the clamps and the editor both ask it, and the test keeps its independent reading only as an explicit cross-check that the two views of a skeleton agree.

AND THE 'ONE RULE FOR BOTH' WAS WRONG. Unifying the two clamps first produced a single sign rule -- 'folding brings the end toward the limb's root' -- which is true and DEGENERATE ON A STRAIGHT LIMB: cross(axis, lower) is perpendicular to the bone while (root - end) lies along it, so the dot product is exactly 0.0 on make_full_rig and the knee clamp silently answered 'no axis'. It reads as a knee clamp that does nothing. A knee is judged against the body's forward, an elbow against the root; the sign follows the same source as the axis, for the same reason.

7 of 7 mutations red, baseline green, source restored byte-for-byte from a snapshot rather than a checkout. TWO of the seven survived their first run and each named a fixture that could not reach its subject: deleting the 5-degree rest-bend floor changed no verdict, because the only straight-arm rig was EXACTLY 180 degrees and the zero-cross-product guard caught it either way (fixed with a rig bent 2 degrees -- real to the arithmetic, meaningless as intent); and deleting the elbow clamp's own bone filter changed no verdict, because 'the elbow rule leaves knees alone' ran on a rig with NO LEGS. That test now asserts the knee is answerable AND that its probe delta is illegal for the knee, so being left alone cannot be confused with being legal already.

WHAT REMAINS DIFFERENT FROM UNITY, stated rather than left to be found: Unity's Avatar Configure window lets a rigger EDIT the muscle axes and hinge frames by hand; this engine derives them and refuses where the rig does not carry the answer. That is a smaller authoring surface, not a missing capability -- the derivation, the clamp and the refusal are all there, and the refusal is visible in the editor. The three gaps this row named for two weeks -- no IK, no muscle-space clamping, no per-bone twist redistribution -- are all closed, and the runtime does retarget per frame (jce_sr_anim_retarget.c), which was the original reason this row said 'behind'.

features.feature: Separate early-reflection and late-reverb levels
features.evidence: THE ROW SAID ONE MISSING EARLY/LATE SPLIT. Counting what actually reached the DSP found SIX authored numbers that did nothing: jce_audio_set_reverb read five of JceAudioReverbParams's nine fields -- room_size, diffusion, density and pre_delay_ms reached no part of the DSP -- and the scene component's `reflections` and `reflectionsDelay` were parsed, written back, drawn in the inspector, and reached no preset field at all. The public header said 'room_size (m) scales the pre-delay' while there was no pre-delay, and called diffusion/density 'accepted for completeness'. A room answers a sound three times -- direct, off its nearest surfaces, then as a diffuse tail -- and this produced only the third, starting immediately, which is why every room sounded like the same room at a different volume. The DSP now has a per-channel delay line tapped twice (the late tail's PRE-DELAY and the EARLY reflection), and diffusion drives the allpass feedback, which is what diffusion is. density stays unread and is now the only field described that way: it would mean a variable comb count and a fixed network cannot express it. MEASURED AS AN IMPULSE RESPONSE, which is the only way to tell 'the tail is delayed' from 'the tail is quieter'. Seven cases: the tail's energy before a 60 ms pre-delay drops below 5% of the tail's; room_size 34 m derives ~100 ms of it at 0.34 m per ms, the rate the header always claimed; an explicit pre-delay beats the derived one; the early tap appears at its stated delay and DISAPPEARS at early_mix 0 while the tail stays (the control that separates 'the tap exists' from 'something is loud'); its level is proportional; diffusion 0.2 vs 0.8 change the response while 0.5 reproduces Freeverb's fixed value BIT FOR BIT, so the new parameter did not silently re-tune every existing preset; and two runs are identical. Verified by ablation: removing the early tap fails exactly the two early cases, removing the pre-delay fails exactly the two delay cases. NONE OF THAT COULD BE ASSERTED BEFORE, because the reverb had no offline entry point -- the DSP chain beside it has had one since it was written, for this exact reason ('the same math runs offline over a known PCM buffer, which is how the effects are unit-tested with no audio device'). jce_audio_reverb_process_offline is that door. The inspector's unread badge on `reflections` came off with the fix, and the existing test that PINNED the two together -- 'if this fails the field is now read and its unwired badge must come off' -- did exactly that. Its case was rewritten to guard the new decision rather than deleted: what a test guards should move with the code.

features.feature: Always Included Shaders reach the cook
features.evidence:
SHIPPED 2026-09-07.  Unity's setting exists because a shader named only from a SCRIPT is reachable from no material and gets stripped.  The same is true here of a graph-compiled .bin blob, or of any asset a script names by string: no scene, material or descriptor points at it, so the packer's dependency closure never sees it and the shipped game asks for a file that was never packed.

The packer already had the mechanism -- bundle_roots.json, an optional document of 'assets nothing points at but the game needs' -- and the missing half was a way for the PROJECT SETTING to reach it.  JceBundlePackOptions gained an always_included list (APPENDED; NULL/0 is the historical behaviour exactly) which the packer stages as dependency ROOTS, so the fixed-point closure follows whatever they reference.  MERGED with bundle_roots.json rather than replacing it: a project may reasonably declare both, and a list that silently won over the other would be a shipped build missing exactly what somebody thought they had declared.  The editor snapshots the multiline setting on the main thread with everything else the worker reads.

A PATH THAT RESOLVES TO NOTHING FAILS THE RUN, not warns.  The whole reason the list exists is that nothing else names these assets, so nothing else would ever have caught the typo -- it would have surfaced at runtime, on a player's machine, as a script asking for a shader that was never packed.

TESTED in tests/os/resource/test_jce_bundle_pack.c (NOT IN THE TREE -- tests/ is gitignored on this branch), which packs the same scene three times: WITHOUT the list the unreferenced blob does not appear in the dependency graph (the control -- without it, a packer that happened to sweep the directory would satisfy the next assertion for free), WITH the list it does, and a name that resolves to nothing makes the run exit non-zero.  The negative control -- disabling the staging loop -- turns the test red.

Also here, because the change pushed jce_bundle_pack.c across 3000 lines and this tree answers a FIRST crossing by splitting rather than raising: the in-process asset cook moved to jce_bundle_pack_cook.c (2985 -> 2701 + 319).  The seam is not arbitrary -- packing is two jobs, working out WHICH assets travel and turning each into its shipped BYTES, and the second is where every slow second of a build goes, is the only part that fans out onto the job pool, and reaches the first through exactly THREE names.  That count is the measure of whether it was a seam or a cut.
features.compared: Unity's Always Included Shaders, which is a list of shaders forced into every build because nothing references them.  JCE's is a list of ASSETS with the same job and the same failure mode; it is more general (a script can name any asset by string, not only a shader) and stricter (an unresolvable entry fails the build rather than being dropped).

features.feature: Gamma / Linear colour space selection
features.evidence:
SHIPPED 2026-09-07, in two halves, and the FIRST half was a defect rather than a missing knob.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG.  The engine decoded sRGB in the SHADER -- pow(2.2) on s_albedo, on s_emissive and on fs_terrain's four layer albedos -- so the GPU filtered FIRST.  Bilinear taps and every mip level are averaged by fixed-function hardware on the ENCODED values, and only then did the shader decode.  Averaging is a linear-space operation; doing it in a non-linear space is the wrong answer, worst where a texture is minified, which is most of the frame.  Unity, UE and Godot all sample albedo through a hardware sRGB view.  And pow(2.2) is not the sRGB transfer function: the real curve has a linear toe below 0.04045 and diverges most in the darks.

Both are one fix: BGFX_TEXTURE_SRGB at creation plus deleting the shader's decode, landed together because either alone is a full stop of error in one direction.  Scope is exactly the samplers that decoded -- sprites, particles, UI, cookies and masks do not, so flagging their textures would wash them out; the plain resolver stays the default, so a site nobody converted keeps its old behaviour and a double decode is unreachable.  Wired at the MeshRenderer albedo/emissive slots (three paths each), the material-path fallback, the terrain layer albedos, the texture-array instancing atlas (its blit is a raw byte copy -- an unflagged array would have rendered over-bright while the solo path beside it stayed correct) and the glTF loader, which now states the colour space PER SLOT as glTF 2.0 5.19 does.  The scene cache and the editor's asset cache key on the colour space, because one PNG can be an albedo here and a mask there.

THEN THE SETTING.  Project Settings > Graphics > Color Space is now authoritative: jce_texture_set_colour_space decides BOTH the hardware sRGB decode and the output encode exponent (u_iblParams.z, the one free component, read by all seven LDR encodes) and the tonemap gamma, so the decode and the encode cannot disagree.  Applied at the same seam the anisotropic setting already uses, and again the moment the combo changes -- the viewport beside it is the only way to judge the choice.

srgb_write IS GONE.  It was a second bool for the ENCODE half of the same decision, and its own baseline entry said so: 'it cannot be decided separately ... wiring one without the other gives a project that decodes linear and writes linear, which is a double-darkened image nobody asked for.'  A knob that can only hold the value the other knob implies is not a setting.  Unity ships one Color Space combo; UE and Godot 4 ship neither, being linear-only.

MEASURED (D3D11, editor scene view, envshot).  The flag reaches the GPU: same build with the sRGB view forced off while the shaders keep their decode removed -- 509,710 px (47.58%), mean +6.25 BRIGHTER, against a 12,513 px (1.17%) floor.  The shipped delta from the old shader-decode build: 271,800 px (25.37%), mean 0.366 -- small, as it must be, and the strong part LOCALISED (5,826 px past 16/255 against 465 px of noise at the same threshold, 12.5x, in one region of textured terrain; a global shift would have meant a polarity error).  The two MODES: Gamma vs Linear on the same build changes 1,039,380 px (97.02%), mean 17.92, max 112, against a 25,035 px (2.34%) floor -- which is what this row's own settings-baseline entry demanded before it could close ('proving the two look different on a measured A/B ... a colour-space knob that changes nothing is worse than no knob').

The settings gate was reproduced red: removing the three jce_texture_set_colour_space calls makes check_project_settings_consumed fail with 'authored in Project Settings, serialised, and read by NOTHING outside the panel and the serialiser'.

Two instrument failures on the way, recorded because they cost the most time: a purpose-built fixture whose ground plane and model carried NO textures (a probe showed the texture-creation path was never entered, and the control moved 1/255), and a first Gamma A/B that wrote color_space at the JSON root instead of under `graphics` -- the setter logged LINEAR 1060 times while the file said 0.
features.compared: Unity's Player Settings Color Space (Gamma/Linear) -- JCE now matches it, with both modes real and measurably different.  UE and Godot 4 are linear-only and expose no such setting; JCE's Linear default is theirs.  All three sample albedo through a hardware sRGB view, which is the half of this row that was a defect rather than a missing control.

features.feature: Camera stacking / overlay cameras
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-07 and MEASURED. JceCameraComponent.stack_index is read: 0 is the base camera (the primary), 1..3 are OVERLAY cameras drawn on top of it in that order, each with its own transform, lens, culling mask and clear mode, into the base camera's colour target. Resolved by jce_scene_camera_resolve_stack (two cameras sharing a stack_index is refused as AMBIGUOUS, exactly as two primaries already were -- what a player sees on top must not be ECS iteration order) and drawn by jce_scene_renderer_render_camera_overlay, wired in the editor Game View AND in jce_default_main's two render paths, at the same place.
THE VIEW ORDER IS THE FEATURE. The overlays get a named, base-relative band (base+64..66, frozen range [5]) that the view-order builder places AFTER the base camera's whole contiguous run and BEFORE every consumer of the colour it produced. After the whole run because base+16/17 -- the fog composite and the underwater absorption -- DRAW INTO that colour, and an overlay ahead of them comes back fogged by the base camera's atmosphere. Before the consumers because the filler tail is ascending id order, which would put base+64 after SSR (base+18), the project fullscreen chain (base+20..25), SSGI's composite (base+27) and the PostFX chain (base+30) -- an overlay composited onto a tone-mapped image, the one thing a camera stack is defined not to be.
MEASURED (base camera masked to layer 0 sees a sphere; an overlay camera masked to layer 5 sees a cube 30 m behind it, from its own viewpoint; editor Game View in Play, D3D11, envshot --play; noise floor = the same build twice, 0 px in all four measured boxes):
  overlay ON vs the overlay's stack_index set to 0 (so it is neither primary nor an overlay, and renders nothing): the cube's box changes 100%, mean 46.954, peak 120/255. Sphere, ground and sky: 0 px each.
  NO-OP CONTROL: an overlay masked to a layer with nothing on it and clearing NOTHING is byte-identical to no overlay at all -- 0 px in every box -- with the machinery fully active (band reserved, order changed, a second scene render executed).
  CLEAR MODE IS READ: with the overlay camera moved 40 m from the cube so its depth exceeds the base scene's, DEPTH_ONLY and NOTHING differ (3.3% of the cube's box, mean 1.572, peak 90) and are identical everywhere else. Without that variant the fixture could not tell the two modes apart, and the first run of this measurement could not either.
  SKYBOX ON AN OVERLAY IS REFUSED and logged once, drawn as DEPTH_ONLY: identical to DEPTH_ONLY, 0 px. A sky drawn by an overlay covers the base camera entirely, which is a replacement, not a stack; Unity refuses it too.
TWO DEFECTS THE CONTROLS CAUGHT, both in the wiring rather than the feature:
  (1) The overlay's second scene render was SUBMITTED after the base render, so it was the last one to set per-frame renderer state -- and the editor's fog/SSR composite and fullscreen-effect passes run after that and read it. An overlay that cleared nothing and drew nothing moved 47% of the pixels around every silhouette. Overlays are now submitted FIRST and drawn LAST (bgfx orders by view, not by submission), the same rule the planar reflection's own call site records. The no-op control is what found it; the first explanation offered for it -- a depth clear reaching passes that still read depth -- was wrong, and the ordering change made for that reason survives on the correct one.
  (2) JCE_VIEW_SR_OFFSET_RESERVED, the macro the editor's static_asserts call to ask 'may a foreign pass take base+N', tested frozen ranges 0..3 and stopped. Range [4] -- SSGI's 26/27, appended earlier the same day -- was in the frozen set, counted by JCE_VIEW_SR_FROZEN_RANGE_COUNT and checked by check_view_reservations.py, and the C macro still answered 'go ahead'. Found by adding range [5] and asserting it; both ranges now have clauses and both have static_asserts.
SCOPE: three overlays, because stack_index documents 1..3; a fourth is warned about once rather than dropped in silence. An overlay renders reduced (reduced_pass): no shadows of its own, no screen-space effects, no post -- the base camera's chain runs on the finished stack, which is what Unity does with one volume stack per camera. Its own viewport slot (JCE_SR_VIEWPORT_SLOTS 4 -> 7) so an overlay's previous-frame camera never overwrites a viewport's.
features.compared: Unity URP camera stacking; UE composure

features.feature: Inspect generated and compiled shader code for a material
features.evidence: Shader Inspector, a tab of the Graph Authoring workbench (editor/src/panels/jce_panel_shader_inspector.cpp), plus the same answers headlessly: `python scripts/jce.py shader-inspect <file.sc> --backend d3d11|vulkan|opengl|gles|metal [--json] [--code]`. THREE THINGS, from three places. (1) Preprocessed source, every backend, via shaderc --preprocess -- the pane that answers whether an #include or a #define actually reached the file. (2) Reflection, every backend: the uniform table, the vertex attribute list and the code size, parsed out of the bgfx blob by the new public jce_shader_reflect() (engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_shader_reflect.h). The layout was read off real blobs, not from memory -- the per-uniform record is ten bytes after the name, not six, and the attribute trailer is absent from GLSL fragment blobs; either assumption produces plausible garbage rather than an error. (3) Compiled code: for GLSL/ESSL the blob's code section IS the post-optimiser source and is shown verbatim; for DirectX, shaderc --disasm (which writes <out>.bin.disasm, not stdout) gives DXBC assembly and jce_shader_disasm_stats() classifies it. MEASURED on this tree's own shaders: engine/shaders/pbr/fs_pbr.sc at s_5_0 -O3 reports 8188 instructions (4514 arithmetic, 1061 texture, 2613 flow) and 64 uniforms -- 16 samplers in slots 0..15, which is the sampler ceiling this tree had only ever asserted in prose, now machine-readable. fs_composite.sc: 1395 instructions. LIMIT, stated in the UI rather than hidden: instruction counts come from a DirectX disassembly because that is the only per-instruction listing bgfx's shaderc produces; on Vulkan/Metal the panel reports the count as UNAVAILABLE rather than as zero. The disassembler's own "Approximately N instruction slots used" line is deliberately not used: measured at -O0 and -O3 on fs_composite it says 0 both times. One parser, not two: the panel and the host tool both call the engine's functions, and the tool's --self-test (which builds a blob byte by byte and requires EVERY truncation of it to be refused) runs as a POST_BUILD step, so it cannot become another self-test with no caller. Negative control: removing the two trailing per-uniform fields makes that build fail with three named complaints.

AHEAD of all three on one axis: none of them can be asked from a terminal, and this one can (jce.py shader-inspect --json), which is what a CI regression check or an assistant needs.

features.feature: Choose additive or multiply blending on a material
features.evidence:
A public enum for it exists and nothing consumes it. engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_gfx_types.h:77-82 declares JceBlendMode { JCE_BLEND_NONE, JCE_BLEND_ALPHA, JCE_BLEND_ADD, JCE_BLEND_MULTIPLY } and it is shipped in the SDK. I grepped the whole tree for JceBlendMode, JCE_BLEND_ADD, JCE_BLEND_MULTIPLY and JCE_BLEND_NONE: the only hits are the header itself and its five copies under dist/*/sdk/include — zero uses in engine/, editor/, scripting/ or the user projects. This is built-but-unwired; the missing reader is any function taking a JceBlendMode. The real material path hard-codes one blend: jce_pbr_material_render_state (engine/src/renderer/jce_pbr_material.c:150-167) emits only SRC_ALPHA/INV_SRC_ALPHA for JCE_ALPHA_BLEND, so additive glass, multiply decals and premultiplied alpha cannot be authored on a material at all.  || ADVERSARIALLY VERIFIED: a second agent was told to REFUTE this claim by finding the implementation, because this repository has been wrong about 'behind'/'absent' twice (auto-LOD, read off a truncated grep; script hot-reload, where interpreted scripts DO reload every Play). Verdict: claim stands -- CLAIM STANDS — I could not find an implementation, and the absence is deeper than the claimant said.

WHAT I SEARCHED (not just grep counts — I read every candidate file): JceBlendMode, JCE_BLEND_*, blend_mode/blendMode/BlendMode, additive/multiply/premultiplied, alphaMode/alpha_mode, surfaceType/renderMode, BGFX_STATE_BLEND_FUNC, JCE_STATE_BLEND_FUNC, plus engine/shaders/pbr/ (53 files), tools/, scripts/, contracts/script-api.json, the editor material viewer + material/shader graph, and authored .mat.json assets in caged_kingdom/.

1. The dead enum is worse than reported. engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_gfx_types.h:70-82 is a two-enum block titled "Render state enums (engine-owned, maps to bgfx internally)". BOTH are dead: `grep -rn "JceCullMode\|JceBlendMode" engine editor scripting tools scripts caged_kingdom` returns exactly two lines — jce_gfx_types.h:75 and :82, their own closing braces. The claimant only checked the blend half. And it is frozen: contracts/abi-snapshot.txt:47 records the enum in a TRACKED contract, so it ships and cannot quietly disappear.

2. The missing piece is not "a reader" — it is the storage. JceBlendMode is a naked type: no struct field anywhere has that type. JcePbrMaterial (engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_pbr_material.h:40-90) has alpha_mode/alpha_cutoff/double_sided/render_priority/custom_program and no blend member; JceAlphaMode (:30-34) is exactly OPAQUE/MASK/BLEND. JceMeshRenderer mirrors it — engine/include/jce/middleware/scene/jce_scene.h:84 `int alpha_mode; /* 0=OPAQUE, 1=MASK, 2=BLEND */`. So adding "a function taking a JceBlendMode" would fix nothing; the field, the file schema, the scene component, the editor UI and the state function all have to be added.

3. Every mesh draw in the tree gets one blend func. engine/src/renderer/jce_pbr_material.c:143-168 — jce_pbr_material_render_state emits only BGFX_STATE_BLEND_FUNC(SRC_ALPHA, INV_SRC_ALPHA) at :154-155. It is the sole state source for meshes: engine/src/middleware/scene/jce_sr_draw.c:2249, :2363, :3017, :5364 and engine/src/middleware/scene/jce_sr_environment.c:1044. `grep -n "BLEND" jce_sr_draw.c` returns one hit — a comment at :5360.

4. The custom-shader escape hatch does NOT reach it. engine/src/middleware/scene/jce_sr_draw.c:5364-5375: mat_state is computed from jce_pbr_material_render_state BEFORE the graph program is selected, so a Shader Graph "Compile & Bind" material still draws under src-alpha/inv-src-alpha fixed-function blend. There is no blend/surface-type setting in editor/src/shadergraph/* or editor/src/panels/material_graph/* (grep for blend there returns only the "Multiply (Color/Float)" math NODES at jce_shadergraph_registry.cpp:88-89).

5. The file format cannot express it. engine/src/renderer/jce_pbr_material.c:569-575 parses "alphaMode" as MASK / BLEND / else OPAQUE; the save side (:648-651) writes the same three. No "blend", "blendMode", "renderMode" or "surfaceType" key is read or written. Authored assets confirm it — caged_kingdom/halloween-test/Materials/M_Universal_Glass.mat.json has no blend key, and no .mat.json in the tree does. engine/src/middleware/scene/jce_scene_components_json.c:1057 reads `alphaMode` as a plain int, default 0.

6. The editor offers exactly three choices. editor/src/viewers/jce_fv_material.cpp:183-187 builds a 3-item array and :250-254 drives `ImGui::Combo("##alpha", &alpha_idx, alpha_items, 3)` with alpha_idx clamped to 0..2. i18n agrees across all 15 locales — only inspector.alphaMode.opaque/.mask/.blend exist (editor/resources/assets/i18n/en.json:2073-2076).

7. Additive exists in the engine but never on a material, and multiply exists nowhere author-facing. Particles: engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_particles.h:155-158 (`bool blend_alpha`) and engine/src/renderer/jce_gpu_particles.c:450-452 — a bool, alpha-vs-additive, no multiply. Fullscreen effects: engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_fullscreen_effect.h:26-30 JceFullscreenEffectBlend, applied at engine/src/renderer/jce_fullscreen_effect.c:766-769. Internal compositing only: jce_ssr.c:251, jce_volumetric_fog.c:374, jce_underwater.c:134-137. Decals are hard-coded alpha too (engine/src/renderer/jce_decals.c:321), so the claimant's "multiply decals" example is unreachable by a second independent path.

8. Nearest thing that could be mistaken for a rebuttal — and why it isn't. engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_lowlevel.h:206-217 defines JCE_BLEND_ZERO/ONE/SRC_ALPHA/INV_SRC_ALPHA/DST_COLOR + JCE_STATE_BLEND_FUNC + jce_set_state(), so C code CAN build ONE/ONE or DST_COLOR/ZERO per draw. These names dodge the claimant's grep (they are JCE_BLEND_ONE, not JCE_BLEND_ADD). But this is an immediate-mode escape hatch below the material system: it is not a material property, it does not serialize to .mat.json, it is not in the editor, and it is not scriptable (contracts/script-api.json has zero blend entries). The only in-tree caller using a non-alpha func is the editor's own overlay, editor/src/scene/jce_scene_render_draw.cpp:1682 (ONE/ONE). So it does not let a user author additive glass on a material.

VERDICT: absent, correctly. Additive glass, multiply decals and premultiplied alpha cannot be authored on a material — not because a reader is missing, but because no material blend field exists at any of the six layers (public struct, render-state builder, .mat.json schema, scene component, editor UI, i18n). The shipped JceBlendMode enum is a type with no storage and no consumer, and the same block's JceCullMode is dead the same way. Note: this is a static read of the tree at HEAD on branch audit-p0-fixes-2026-08-31; I did not build or run the engine, which is appropriate here since the finding is about API/format surface, not runtime behavior.  || CLOSED 2026-09-06, and the enum was the smallest part of it. jce_pbr_material_render_state now emits SRC_ALPHA/ONE for ADD and DST_COLOR/ZERO for MULTIPLY; blend_mode is on JcePbrMaterial and on JceMeshRenderer, round-trips as `blendMode`, and the Inspector shows the combo only under BLEND, the only mode that consults it.
THE REASON IT COULD NOT BE DEMONSTRATED AT FIRST: a glTF model's render state never came from its material. THREE places owned it and all three hard-coded BGFX_STATE_DEFAULT -- two submits in jce_model.c and jce_skinned_mesh_submit, whose own comment records the same class of bug being fixed once before for double_sided. For an OPAQUE material the two are the same bits, which is why nobody noticed: a model's FACTORS arrived through jce_pbr_material_bind while its alpha mode and blend equation arrived nowhere, so a model could not be transparent at all. Four pine models with alphaMode BLEND and alpha 0.6 rendered fully opaque and correctly TINTED by their base colours -- that picture is exactly the factors arriving without the state. Forcing additive inside render_state changed nothing, which is what said the function was not the one being consulted. jce_skinned_mesh's bool double-sided override is now the whole state (same global, widened, no new file-scope state).
MEASURED (d3d11, four pine models, frame 300):
  floor                        1499 px (0.140%)  mean 0.000
  opaque vs BLEND            446743 px (41.70%)  mean 26.671
  alpha vs ADDITIVE          505829 px (47.21%)  mean 9.442
  alpha vs MULTIPLY          446960 px (41.72%)  mean 5.477
Three mutually distinct equations, each about 300x the floor. SAFETY CONTROL: caged_kingdom/hidden_cove, an all-opaque production scene, is unchanged by the state fix -- 3366 px (0.314%) against its own floor.
features.compared: Godot's BaseMaterial3D has blend_mode Mix/Add/Sub/Mul on every material. UE's translucent materials pick Blend Mode Translucent/Additive/Modulate/AlphaComposite. Unity shaders set Blend One One (additive) or Blend DstColor Zero (multiply) per pass, and URP/HDRP surface options expose Alpha/Premultiply/Additive/Multiply directly.

features.feature: Material assets that inherit from a parent material
features.evidence:
SHIPPED 2026-09-07.  A .mat.json may name a `parent`; the child starts from it and states only its overrides.

WHAT LANDED.  The loader became recursive (depth cap 8, cycle guard on the path chain with separators normalised and case folded, so a\B and a/b are one path).  The parent is resolved against the CHILD's directory, like the texture and shader-blob paths, so a chain works from any cwd.  A missing or cyclic parent is a warning and the child still loads with its own values -- a broken link must not turn a saved material into the defaults.

THE HALF THAT WOULD HAVE LIED.  Half this loader already read `(double)out->field` (the UV transform, blend mode, stencil block) and half read a LITERAL: metallic 0.0, roughness 1.0, def_bc white, def_em black, normalScale 1.0, aoStrength 1.0, alphaCutoff 0.5, renderPriority 0, doubleSided false.  With a parent in place a literal is not `the default', it is `discard what the parent said' -- and it still renders, just as the wrong material.  Every one of them is now the inherited current value.

THE OTHER HALF.  Every caller rewrites the whole file from a JcePbrMaterial, which has no parent field, so `parent' joined the saver's keep[] preserve list -- without it the first Save severs the link and leaves an unrelated copy that still looks like a variant.  And the saver now REMOVES every key whose value equals the parent's, so the child records overrides only; write the resolved set instead and editing the parent stops reaching the child, which is a feature that works exactly once.

THE SHIPPED PATH.  jce_bundle_deps.c's kAssetKeys[] gained "parent".  The packer learns that a JSON string names a file from that table and `parent' does not look like a path, so the key that most needs collecting was the one most likely to be missed -- and the failure is silent: the built game loads the child, cannot find the parent, and renders the overrides over the DEFAULTS.  Right in the editor, wrong in the exe.  The packer's fixed-point descriptor closure then carries a whole chain.

AUTHORING.  The material viewer gained a Parent Material row (written through the file and re-resolved at once, because the values below it are the resolved ones and do not exist until the link is on disk), plus a hint that saving stores only what differs.  The asset browser gained Create Variant on a .mat.json -- deliberately not Duplicate: a copy is a second material that drifts, a variant follows its parent forever.  Two public functions, jce_pbr_material_get_parent / _set_parent, both through the FILE rather than the struct, which is a resolved render state copied by value on every draw.  25+3 i18n keys across all 15 locales.

MEASURED (D3D11, editor scene view, envshot, static fixture, noise floor 498 px / 0.046%).  A cube with the PARENT material vs the same cube with an EMPTY CHILD of it: 581 px, at the floor -- pixel-identical.  Same cube with an EMPTY material that has NO parent: 92,536 px (8.64%), mean 3.54 -- so `empty file' is not accidentally the same thing and the child really took its values from the parent.  Same cube with a child that overrides base colour and emissive: 92,520 px, mean 4.60.  Three constructions, three distinct outcomes.

UNIT TEST (tests/renderer/test_jce_material_inherit.c, NOT IN THE TREE -- tests/ is gitignored on this branch).  The picture cannot say that a child stating ONE key keeps the rest, that a chain resolves, that a cycle does not hang, that Save keeps the link and stores only overrides, or that the packer ships the parent.  Five negative controls each turned it red on the assertion that names the defect: never loading the parent, restoring one literal default (roughness), dropping `parent' from keep[], disabling the override differ (which failed on `the parent's new roughness did not reach the saved child' -- the exact half-feature), and dropping `parent' from kAssetKeys.

GATE REPAIR.  check_bundle_deps_keys.py stayed GREEN through all of this: it asked `does this key LOOK like a file?' and `parent' does not.  A gate that only fires on shapes it already knows cannot catch the shape nobody thought of, which is the only kind that ever ships.  It is now inverted -- every material key must appear in a JUDGED table with a verdict, and an unjudged key FAILS -- and it reads four key sources instead of one (json_string reads, jce_json_set_string writes, the keep[] list, the kTexKeys alias table), because a read-only view called `shaderGraph' stale and would have invited its removal.  Both new failure modes were reproduced.
features.compared: UE's Material Instances: a parent plus a child overriding only exposed parameters, instance-of-instance chains, runtime MIDs.  JCE matches the asset half (parent link, chains, override-only storage) and not the runtime MID half -- the per-entity equivalent is JceMeshRenderer's material_override_mask, which is a different mechanism.  Unity's Material Variants and Godot's next_pass layering are the same asset-level idea.

features.feature: Materials support clearcoat, anisotropy, sheen or subsurface
features.evidence: ALL FOUR NOW. Clearcoat and sheen shipped earlier; this adds anisotropy and translucency. THE ROW'S OWN REASON FOR NOT SHIPPING ANISOTROPY WAS WRONG: it said the lobe needs a per-material tangent frame the shading path does not carry, and fs_pbr_main.sh builds a TBN from v_tangent/v_bitangent for normal mapping three lines above the specular lobe. It is glTF's KHR_materials_anisotropy -- a strength and a rotation in turns -- with the anisotropic GGX distribution and the isotropic visibility term, the trade Filament documents for its mobile tier and the right one against a stated integrated-GPU baseline. It REPLACES the isotropic highlight for that light rather than adding to it, so there is no round core inside the stretched lobe, and strength 0 is exactly the untouched shader. TRANSLUCENCY, NOT SUBSURFACE, and named after what it is: wrap-free back transmission driven by one thickness scalar -- Frostbite's model, what Godot 4 does at its cheap end and Unity calls Translucent. The subsurface half of the old row stands: a diffusion profile with a thickness map is a subsystem, and on this baseline it is the wrong one. Naming it translucency leaves a future diffusion profile free to arrive as its own thing instead of as a redefinition of this number. MEASURED against a noise floor of 0 px / peak 1 (same build, two runs): anisotropy 0.9 moves 4908 px peak 145, and ROTATING it a quarter turn moves 2003 px more -- the control that separates a live rotation from a field that is read and discarded. Translucency was swept over four light directions rather than asserted: 84343 px peak 197 when the object is between the light and the viewer, and EXACTLY 0 px in the other three. A back-transmission term that fires in every direction would not be one. TWO REAL DEFECTS THE CONTROLS CAUGHT, neither visible by reading: the first version split the PERCEPTUAL roughness where distributionGGX squares its argument internally, making the narrow axis about four times sharper than the lobe it replaces and turning the highlight into fireflies; and it called normalize() on a zero tangent. Which is how the third thing was found -- THE STANDARD MESH LAYOUT HAS NO TANGENT ATTRIBUTE at all (jce_mesh.c: position, normal, texcoord0), so every primitive arrives with a zero tangent. Anisotropy builds a stable Duff-et-al. basis from the normal when there is none, which the rotation then steers; the same absence makes NORMAL MAPPING inert on every primitive, which is a different feature and is recorded as its own row. Both lobes are hashed into the material key AND into JceSrPrimMaterialSignature (6 -> 13 floats), because an instanced run issues ONE uniform upload for the whole batch. Inspector rows in all 15 locales. jce_pbr_material.c's nine separate uniform-handle statics became one struct on the way -- nine globals is nine, and the dedup audit counted them: 859 -> 853, improved by six.
features.compared: Unity HDRP, UE and Godot 4 ship all four

features.feature: A normal map works on any mesh
features.evidence: OPENED AND CLOSED THE SAME DAY, and the version of this row I wrote an hour earlier WAS WRONG in a way worth keeping. It said a normal map on a primitive 'changes no pixels'. Measured against a noise floor of 0 px: normalScale 1 vs 0 on a normal-mapped sphere moved 4284 px, peak 44. So the map WAS being applied. The real defect was worse than inert. The standard vertex layout in jce_mesh.c declared POSITION, NORMAL and TEXCOORD0 and no TANGENT, while vs_pbr.sc reads a_tangent and writes v_tangent from it -- so on every non-skinned mesh the fragment shader's tangent frame came from an UNBOUND vertex attribute, and what a backend leaves there is undefined. All three observed outcomes are wrong and which one a project gets depends on its backend: BLACK on WebGL2 (recorded in fs_pbr_main.sh's own comment -- the space demo's procedural Earth beside glTF models that did carry tangents -- and the reason its dot(Tin,Tin) > 1e-8 guard exists), silently SKIPPED where that guard catches it, and on D3D11 APPLIED THROUGH A FRAME THAT IS NOT THE SURFACE'S, which is the one that looks like it works. Proved by ablation rather than by reading: forcing that branch off made the normal-mapped sphere identical to the same sphere with no normal map (0 px), so the branch was running. FIXED AT THE FUNNEL. JceMeshVertex gains tangent[4] (xyz + bitangent sign, glTF's layout) and jce_mesh_create GENERATES the frame -- Lengyel accumulation, Gram-Schmidt against the vertex normal, handedness from the cross product -- when the caller supplied none. That is glTF's own rule, and jce_mesh_create is where primitives, imported models, terrain chunks and static-batch merges all become a mesh, so it fixes the class rather than four instances. A vertex whose UV gradient is degenerate (a sphere's poles) takes a stable Duff-et-al. basis from its normal rather than a zero. THREE-WAY MEASUREMENT: after the fix, normal map vs none is 10493 px peak 79 -- 2.4x what the fictitious frame produced; the same normal-mapped render CHANGED by 10779 px against its own pre-fix self, which is what 'it was computed in the wrong frame' looks like; and a mesh with NO normal map is 0 px different, which is the control that says adding a tangent to every vertex perturbed nothing else. Anisotropy now takes the real UV tangent instead of its fallback and follows the sphere's latitude. Cost: 16 bytes per vertex on every non-skinned mesh. The dedup audit caught the layout becoming a second copy of the skinned one within the same change (similar-code 67 -> 68); there is one definition now, and the extraction is pixel-identical.
features.compared: Unity/UE/Godot generate tangents for meshes that need them

features.feature: Materials can write and test the stencil buffer
features.evidence:
SHIPPED 2026-09-07.  A material now carries the full stencil block and it reaches the GPU, measured rather than argued.

WHAT LANDED.  JcePbrMaterial and JceMeshRenderer each gained SIX appended fields (func / ref / read mask / fail / zfail / pass op) -- not Unity's seven: bgfx's stencil word carries NO write mask, and a seventh field would have been authored, serialised and unreadable, which is the exact defect this ledger exists to find.  jce_pbr_material_stencil() assembles the bgfx word; jce_enc_set_stencil() is the new encoder entry beside jce_enc_set_state.  The word is carried on JceDrawCmd rather than applied in the material bind, because bgfx resets the stencil after EVERY submit exactly as it resets the state (RenderDraw::clear under BGFX_DISCARD_STATE, read in the pinned bgfx source) -- a per-material-run bind would have reached the run's first draw and nothing else.  Issued at all 12 submit sites: the 3 render-queue paths, the primitive- and texture-instancing batches, the two material-cache-overflow inline fallbacks, the solo mesh path, vegetation, and the model / skinned-mesh submits.  blend_mode and the stencil word also joined sr_compute_material_key and rq_can_batch -- neither was in either, so two materials differing only in blend equation could already collapse into one batch that took the first entry's state.  BGFX_CLEAR_STENCIL was added wherever depth is cleared (12 sites): bgfx's depth clear leaves the stencil plane alone, so a pass/fail op would otherwise inherit the previous frame's value and drift instead of fail.

MEASURED (D3D11, editor scene view, envshot).  Positive control -- NEVER on every material: 464,421 px changed (43.35%), mean 10.92, against a 10,904 px (1.02%) two-capture noise floor; the mesh geometry vanishes and terrain, water and sky stay, which is the expected signature.  Negative control -- ALWAYS on every material: 14,701 px (1.37%), at the floor, so arming the stencil with a pass-everything compare is pixel-identical to no stencil at all.  AUTHORING CHAIN -- the same NEVER applied through scene JSON (stencilFunc on each MeshRenderer) instead of a forced value: 464,438 px, 17 px from the forced result and well inside the floor, so the component keys reach the GPU by the same path.  BUFFER STATE -- EQUAL with ref 0 against the cleared buffer: at the floor, i.e. identical to baseline, which is only true if the plane is actually cleared to 0; EQUAL with ref 1: nothing draws.  WRITE PATH -- a static two-cube fixture with the transparent queue's render_priority controlling order: a writer (ALWAYS, pass=REPLACE, ref=1) at priority -100 and a tester (EQUAL, ref=1) at +100, overlapping on screen.  Noise floor 179 px (0.017%).  NEVER on the tester removes its whole silhouette (23,297 px); EQUAL 1 removes 20,907 px and leaves 2,390 -- and the survivors are the strip where the writer had already written 1, which is the write and the compare working together.

UNIT TEST (tests/renderer/test_jce_material_stencil.c, NOT IN THE TREE -- tests/ is gitignored on this branch).  The screenshot cannot say that LESS is not LEQUAL or that INCR saturates where INCR_WRAP rolls, because most wrong mappings still draw A picture.  Asserted on the bgfx word: OFF emits none even with a ref and an op set, all eight compares map to distinct constants, ref and read mask ride their own fields, a zero read mask reads as 0xFF, the three ops land in three different bit fields, and clamp is not wrap.  Three negative controls each turned it red on the naming assertion: swapping INCR/INCR_WRAP, making OFF emit a word, and honouring a zero read mask literally.

features.feature: Per-material texture tiling and offset
features.evidence:
JcePbrMaterial (engine/include/jce/renderer/jce_pbr_material.h:40-89) carries no UV scale or offset, and the .mat.json loader reads none: I read jce_pbr_material.c:505-587 end to end, which parses textures, baseColorFactor, metallic, roughness, emissive, normalScale, aoStrength, alphaCutoff, renderPriority, doubleSided and alphaMode — nothing UV-related. The shader confirms it: every map in engine/shaders/pbr/fs_pbr_body.sh samples raw v_texcoord0 with no transform (lines 945 albedo, 1023 normal, 1060 metal-rough, 1099 AO, 1556 emissive), and no uv/tiling uniform appears in its uniform block (lines 31-393). A repo-wide grep for uvScale/tiling/uv_offset outside terrain, decals, water and particles found nothing on the material path. The only way to tile a texture in JCE is to bake it into the mesh UVs.  || ADVERSARIALLY VERIFIED: a second agent was told to REFUTE this claim by finding the implementation, because this repository has been wrong about 'behind'/'absent' twice (auto-LOD, read off a truncated grep; script hot-reload, where interpreted scripts DO reload every Play). Verdict: claim stands -- Claim stands. I re-verified every strand of their evidence and searched under uvScale/uv_offset/tiling/KHR_texture_transform/texTransform/uvParams/repeat_u/triplanar/mainTextureScale/TilingOffset/uv1_scale across engine/include/jce, engine/src, editor/src, engine/shaders, tools/, scripts/, scripting/ plus git -S history. Confirmed absent: JcePbrMaterial has no UV fields (jce_pbr_material.h:40-89); the loader parses none (jce_pbr_material.c:505-587); no UV uniform is even CREATED -- jce_pbr_material.c:67-70 creates exactly u_baseColorFactor, u_pbrParams, u_emissiveFactor, u_normalScale; all seven PBR vertex shaders are pure pass-through (vs_pbr.sc:15, vs_pbr_inst.sc:27, vs_pbr_inst_fade.sc:28, vs_pbr_inst_tex_array.sc:31, vs_pbr_inst_tint.sc:32, vs_pbr_skinned.sc:52, vs_pbr_skinned_inst.sc:128, each `v_texcoord0 = a_texcoord0;`); JceMeshRenderer's inline material (jce_scene.h:74-129) has no UV field; jce_material_override.h:30-38 defines six override bits, none UV; legacy jce_material.h is texture+tint only.

The one thing they MISSED is real but inert, so it does not lift the status. The editor ships a shader-graph node named literally "UV (Tile/Offset)": editor/src/shadergraph/jce_shadergraph_types.h:38 (NT_UV = 8), editor/src/shadergraph/jce_shadergraph_registry.cpp:44 (socket `{SK_OUTPUT, DT_FLOAT, "Tile"}`) and :92 (ENTRY(NT_UV, "UV (Tile/Offset)", k_uv, nullptr) -- snippet is nullptr), with a live UI control at editor/src/panels/material_graph/jce_material_graph_canvas.cpp:152-158 (ImGui::SliderFloat("##tile", &n.scalar, 0.1f, 16.0f) with its own i18n format string and undo push). THE READER IS MISSING: codegen special-cases NT_UV into the SAME branch as NT_FLOAT (editor/src/shadergraph/jce_shadergraph_codegen.cpp:129-137) and emits only a dangling `float n<id>_o0 = <scalar>;`. The variable it would have to drive is pinned one line above the splice region -- engine/shaders/graph/fs_graph_template.sc:43, `vec2 mat_uv = v_texcoord0;` -- and emit_output (jce_shadergraph_codegen.cpp:163-215) assigns exactly five locals (mat_normal_ts, mat_base_color, mat_metallic, mat_roughness, mat_emissive). `mat_uv` has NO writer anywhere in the repo; the only three references are reads (registry.cpp:87, registry.cpp:91, and the template's own default body). So moving the Tile slider changes one unused float in the generated GLSL and zero pixels.

Two calibration facts: JCE_TEX_WRAP does exist (jce_texture_types.h:30, jce_texture.c:247-249), so their stated workaround -- bake tiling into mesh UVs -- genuinely works; and per-material tiling exists only off the material path, in terrain layers (jce_scene.h:1157 tile_scale) and particle flipbooks (jce_particles.h:309-310 uv_offset/uv_scale), exactly the exclusions they named. Effective user-visible status: absent, with a built-but-unwired editor control that will read as a working feature until someone drags it.  || CLOSED 2026-09-06. uv = mesh_uv * tiling + offset, applied to ALL FIVE maps (albedo, normal, metal-rough, AO, emissive) from one computation in fs_pbr_body.sh; the missing-texture checker keeps raw UVs on purpose, since it exists to show the mesh's own unwrap. The pair lives on JcePbrMaterial (the .mat.json asset) AND on JceMeshRenderer, because the draw path rebuilds a JcePbrMaterial from the component every frame -- a value on the asset alone would be loaded and discarded.
THE HALF THAT WOULD HAVE SHIPPED BROKEN: a glTF model draws with the materials the ASSET carries, and the renderer's material only reaches such a draw when it has an authored albedo or .mat.json. hidden_cove has 1789 mesh renderers and ZERO of either, so the first working version moved 4046 px against a 4339 px floor -- nothing. A positive control (the shader multiplying UVs by 4 unconditionally) moved 159582 px, which is what said the break was CPU-side. Fixed with a per-draw UV override armed like jce_model_set_material_override, plus disqualifying a non-neutral transform from the instanced and meshlet-cull batch paths -- one shared submit binds one material state, so this is the same material divergence those paths already refuse for an override.
MEASURED (d3d11, hidden_cove/beauty, frame 300, tiling 1 -> 4 on all 1789 renderers):
  floor                    5436 px (0.507%)  mean 0.002
  tiling 1 vs 4          158312 px (14.78%)  mean 1.743
  shader-forced control  159582 px (14.90%)  mean 1.743
The authored path and the shader-level control agree to three digits, so the feature reaches exactly the geometry that shader draws and no less. (14.9% is also the share of this frame drawn through fs_pbr_body.sh at all -- terrain, foliage and sky have their own sampling.)
