features.feature: Per-agent height / clearance
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-08. HALF THIS ROW'S EVIDENCE WAS FALSE AND IS CORRECTED HERE. It read: 'The steering agent is 2D and the bake's walkable height is a constant 2.0 for every bake.' The bake height is NOT a constant: the navmesh panel authors it (JceNavMeshBakeConfig.agent_height, default 1.80, edited at jce_panel_navmesh.cpp and written to the sidecar), and it reaches Recast as rcConfig.walkableHeight. Checked before doing any work, because a ledger row that keeps a false mechanism is worse than one that keeps a stale status.
WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE: JceNavAgentComponent.height was documented 'editor gizmo only' and read by NOTHING. So an agent authored at 2.4 m walked a mesh carved for 1.8 m of clearance exactly as if it fitted -- under geometry it could not fit under, with nothing about the steering looking wrong. That is Unity's agent-type model in miniature: a navmesh belongs to the agent it was built for, and an agent that does not match it is not slightly off, it is on the wrong mesh.
THE CLEARANCE WAS ALREADY IN BOTH FILES; NOBODY READ IT BACK. The grid navmesh's settings block has carried agentHeight all along, and Detour's dtCreateNavMeshData writes walkableHeight into the tile header, so it survives into the .navmesh.bin the runtime actually loads (the sidecar .json holds only the bake settings). Two accessors, one per backend, and both compare through the SAME rule -- jce_nav_agent_fits -- so the grid path and the Recast path cannot drift into different ideas of 'too tall'. One warn-once (jce_nav_agent_report_fit) rather than a message per backend.
REPORTED, NOT REFUSED, and the reason is written at the function: refusing would strand the agent where it stands, which is a worse failure than a warning, and the authored intent is usually a mesh that has not been re-baked yet.
THE INTERESTING HALF IS THE TWO UNKNOWNS, and it is what the tests are about. An agent height of 0 is every JceNavAgentDesc written before the field existed; a clearance of 0 is every mesh baked before it was read back. Both mean NO OPINION, not zero -- a check that fired on missing data would reject every scene authored before it existed, which is a worse outcome than the bug it fixes. Four cases: too tall rejects, exactly-the-baked-height fits (the boundary is inclusive, since that is the agent the mesh was carved FOR), an unset agent height never rejects, an unstated clearance never rejects.
WHY 'parity' AND NOT MORE: the steering stays 2D and this does not make an agent duck under a low ceiling -- Unity's does not either; its height feeds the agent cylinder and the agent-type match, which is exactly what this now does. What a 3D crowd would add -- per-agent avoidance cylinders in the VERTICAL axis, and off-mesh links gated on height -- is the dtCrowd feature set, and this engine steers with its own JceNavAvoidanceConfig rather than dtCrowd. That is a separate question from whether the authored height is read, and it is not claimed here in either direction: no row asserts it today and this one does not start.
COMPARED: Unity NavMeshAgent.height + agent types; Recast/Detour rcConfig.walkableHeight and dtCrowdAgentParams.

features.feature: Animator state replication
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-07. jce_net_animator.{h,c} replicates animator state: which state is playing (hashed name), how far into it, at what speed, and up to 8 parameters. Modelled on jce_net_transform.h and DELIBERATELY the same shape -- same register/unregister, same fixed_step + render_step pair, same tick-based interpolation timeline, same authority modes -- because a second networking subsystem with its own vocabulary is two things to learn for one idea.
JceNetAnimatorComponent's THREE KNOBS NOW HAVE A READER. sync_rate_hz, interp_ms and authority_mode round-tripped through the scene file, appeared in the Inspector, and were consulted by nothing anywhere; jce_runtime.c now registers the component with the module and hands it exactly those values, beside the transform block it mirrors. The Inspector's unwired badge came off in the same commit and the panel gained a live readout -- a replication setting you cannot observe is one you cannot tell is working.
THREE THINGS MAKE ANIMATOR STATE DIFFERENT FROM A TRANSFORM, each a bug when unhandled, and each is tested:
  NORMALISED TIME WRAPS. A looping clip runs 0 -> 1 -> 0, so lerping a snapshot at 0.95 towards one at 0.05 the way a position is lerped runs the animation BACKWARDS through the whole clip, once per loop, forever. The interpolator takes the shorter way round. Tested both ways: 0.95 -> 0.05 comes out near the loop point and NOT in the middle of the clip, and -- the negative control -- 0.20 -> 0.60 still interpolates normally, so the wrap handling did not break ordinary interpolation.
  A STATE CHANGE IS NOT A BLEND. Forty per cent of the way from Idle to Jump is not a pose, and neither is a parameter set half from each. Two snapshots naming different states SNAP to the newer one; tested.
  A TRIGGER IS AN EDGE. The state stream is UNRELIABLE by design -- a dropped position snapshot is corrected by the next one, a dropped footstep never fires -- so triggers travel on their own RELIABLE packet and are never inferred from the state stream. Unity's NetworkAnimator splits them for the same reason. The queue drops the OLDEST when full, tested: a queue that discarded NEW triggers would stop responding exactly when the most is happening.
AND: an id that has received nothing returns FALSE rather than a zeroed state, because 'nothing has arrived' is not 'it is idle'.
A COLLISION CAUGHT BY ONE LINE: the trigger packet first took id 8, which is already JCE_REPL_PKT_ACK. The compiler found it only because the dispatch switch happens to name both -- had the two ids stayed in the two files they started in, an ACK and an animator trigger would have been the same packet and nothing would have said so. Both ids now live beside the others they must not collide with, which is the whole registry there is.
WHY 'behind' AND NOT 'parity': the module transports state and nothing SAMPLES an animator into it. jce_net_animator_set_local_state is the authority's push and gameplay has to call it -- deliberately, because a net module that reached up into L5 to read an animation graph would invert the layering jce_net_transform.h is careful to keep, but it does mean a project must write that line. Unity's NetworkAnimator samples the Animator itself. There is also no per-parameter dirty tracking (every snapshot carries all of them) and no cross-fade duration in the wire format, so a receiver snaps where the authority blended.
2026-09-08 -- SOMETHING SAMPLES AN ANIMATOR NOW, without inverting the layering this row was careful about. The net layer still refuses to read an animation graph and is still right to; what it needed was a caller ABOVE both, and the runtime is that -- the same reason it is the thing that consumes the root motion the renderer publishes.
THE PLAYHEAD TRAVELS THE WAY ROOT MOTION ALREADY DID. It lives in the renderer's per-instance animation state, so the renderer publishes it onto JceSkeletalAnimatorComponent.norm_time each frame it evaluates an animator -- appended, 0 until something plays, and normalised and WRAPPING because that is what has to go on the wire: a receiver interpolating 0.95 towards 0.05 can only take the shorter way round the loop if what it receives is a POSITION in the clip rather than seconds into a clip whose length it does not know. That mechanism already existed for rm_valid/rm_dx; this reuses it rather than inventing a second one.
WHAT GOES OUT, and why each: the clip NAME hashed (receivers only compare it, and a string costs bytes every tick forever); the playhead as a position; the speed, so a receiver in slow motion stays in slow motion; and the two blend parameters, because on a blend-tree character they are what decides the pose and a receiver without them plays the right clip at the wrong blend.
SAMPLED BEFORE THE STEP, NOT AFTER. jce_net_animator_fixed_step builds and sends the snapshot from whatever the authority last pushed, so a push placed after it is a tick late forever rather than once.
AUTHORITY IS NOT DECIDED AT THE CALL SITE. set_local_state records what this peer's animator is doing; the module's own is_authority_for decides whether it is broadcast. One answer to 'am I the authority' rather than two that can disagree.
A DEFECT FROM THE ORIGINAL LANDING, FOUND HERE: jce_net_animator_fixed_step was called TWICE per tick -- two lines, one mis-indented, from the commit that first wired the module. fixed_step builds and SENDS a packet, so every animator snapshot went out twice: double the bandwidth for that stream, silently, since a duplicate snapshot is not wrong, only wasteful. Removed.
AND ONE I ALMOST SHIPPED: the sampler first called jce_net_object_id_of(scene, e), a function that does not exist. It COMPILED, through an implicit declaration -- the same C99 hole fixed twice already today in jce_scene.c and jce_ui_canvas_widgets.c. The id is mirrored onto the NetworkObject component at adopt time, which is the field gameplay reads, so there is one answer to 'which net object is this'.
jce_runtime.c is long past the size cap, so the sampler went to a new jce_rt_net.c beside the jce_rt_* family where per-subsystem runtime work already lives; jce_runtime.c gained three lines, which are the call and why it sits where it does.
WHY 'parity' NOW: the transport, the sampler and the authoring surface are all present and the loop is closed. Still not claimed, and unchanged: no per-parameter dirty tracking (every snapshot carries all of them) and no cross-fade duration in the wire format, so a receiver snaps where the authority blended.

features.evidence:

Batched vs unbatched differs on 1.907% of viewport pixels, max 12/255 -- and those pixels carry 7.5x the local gradient of the unchanged ones (3.518 vs 0.470), i.e. they are silhouettes. That is sub-pixel geometry shift from baking world transforms into vertices instead of multiplying by a model matrix in the vertex shader; it is inherent to static batching and Unity's has it too. Flat regions -- where a lighting or material change would show -- do not move.
THE INSTRUMENT HAD TO BE BUILT, and the first two were wrong. bgfx's whole-frame num_draw reads 43 for a scene of 10 props AND 43 for the same scene with 40, so it cannot answer a question about the scene; the render queue's own submits_out is zero here because rq_enabled is 0 (these props do not take the queue path). What was missing was the count of collected entities the colour pass SKIPPED as disabled -- appended to JceSceneCullStats as disabled_skipped -- because a lossless merge draws the same pixels the originals did, so without it a bake that worked and a bake that did nothing produce the same picture and the same entity delta.
TWO DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY, neither this feature's own: (1) EditorMeta.enabled written through the raw component pointer greys the hierarchy row and changes nothing on screen -- jce_scene.h names jce_state_set_entity_enabled as THE entry because the flag is mutated in place and the entry bumps jce_scene_bump_enable_gen for it; (2) JCE_KPI_FRAME_LOG had TWO writers with different schemas on one path -- the engine's all-phase table (which tools/frame_budget.py parses) and the editor's draw-call CSV -- so asking for a draw capture produced a 37,000-line phase table with no num_draw column in it. The editor's is now JCE_KPI_DRAW_LOG.
WHY 'behind' AND NOT 'parity': a merged group culls as ONE object. Unity's Static Batching keeps per-renderer culling by holding index sub-ranges into one shared buffer, so an off-screen member still costs nothing; here the whole group is drawn if any of it is visible, which is why max_vertices splits a group rather than letting it become one un-cullable continent. Unity also has Dynamic Batching, which this does not attempt. Against UE's Merge Actors and Godot 4's MeshInstance3D merge -- both editor-time, both whole-object -- this is equivalent. || 2026-09-17 -- THE SUB-RANGES EXIST AND THE COLOUR PASS USES THEM. The gap this row was behind on was per-renderer culling inside a group: a merged group is one draw, which is the point, and therefore ONE cullable object, so a row of forty fence posts draws all forty whenever any one is on screen. Unity keeps each renderer's index sub-range into the shared buffer; so does this now. jce_mesh_merge_spans reports where each input landed (index range, vertex range, and the WORLD box its transformed vertices actually fill -- from the vertices the merge wrote, not a local bound pushed through the matrix, because the two differ for a sheared or mirrored instance). jce_static_batch_bake writes them beside every group as <stem>.batch.json. The scene renderer probes for it ONCE per model slot (the PAK for a shipped game, the host path in the editor), tests each member's box against the colour pass's OWN frustum planes, coalesces the visible members into runs and submits one draw per run through a per-submit index-range override that the submit itself disarms. || THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES IT A SAVING RATHER THAN A REGRESSION WEARING THE RIGHT NAME: a wholly visible group coalesces to EXACTLY ONE run and takes the path it always took. A coalescer that emitted one submit per member would be correct, would pass every 'is the right geometry drawn' assertion, and would undo the merge. That is the first assertion in the test file and it stands alone. || TESTED: 11 cases, and jce_mesh_merge and jce_static_batch had NO tests at all before them -- a lossless merge that REPLACES geometry in a shipped scene, unexercised. End to end (bake writes two real .glb inputs, merges them, and the loader reads the table back with the second member ten metres along +X in world space); spans (a SKIPPED input keeps its slot, or every span after it would describe the wrong mesh); runs (all visible = 1 run; none = 0; a hole in the middle = 2; out of run slots extends the last run, because drawing more costs time and drawing less is a hole in the world). || STILL BEHIND, and this is what is left: there is no RENDERED measurement. Every layer is proven -- the table is written, read, and turned into the right runs -- but no capture yet shows a baked group on screen submitting fewer indices, because the tree contains no baked group to point a camera at. Until that exists this row does not move; the layers being right is not the same claim as the pixels being right, and this repository has paid for that difference more than once. Unity's Dynamic Batching is also still not attempted. || 2026-09-18 -- THE RENDER-LEVEL MEASUREMENT WAS ATTEMPTED AND IT FOUND THE SEAM IS IN THE WRONG PLACE. A merged group was authored as a fixture (tools/gen_batch_probe_glb.py: eight quads already in world space in one .glb, six metres apart, plus the member table), a scene put in front of a camera, and the probe traced end to end: 'static batch probe: models/batch_probe.glb -> <host>/batch_probe.batch.json => 8 member(s)' and 'carries 8 member(s)'. So the table is found, parsed and cached on the model slot, on a real frame, in the editor. || AND THE CULL NEVER RUNS, because the draw does not go through the seam it was wired into. A diagnostic at SR_DRAW_ONE (jce_sr_draw.c, the solo static-model submit) printed NOTHING for this entity: a lone static glTF model is drawn by the render-queue path instead. That is the remaining work and it is now named rather than assumed -- wire sr_draw_batch_runs into the queue push, not only the solo path. || TWO REAL DEFECTS FELL OUT OF TRYING TO MEASURE IT, neither of which a unit test could have shown: the probe was handed the scene's ASSET-RELATIVE path and looked for the sidecar relative to the editor's working directory, finding nothing silently, every time (fixed: resolve_path, the callback that already exists for the terrain's sidecars); and the fix itself was wrong the first time -- it resolved the SIDECAR path and then handed the loader the unresolved .glb, which derives the sidecar again. features.compared: Unity's Static Batching combines any static renderers sharing a material into one vertex buffer at build time with no geometry or material loss, and Dynamic Batching CPU-transforms small meshes per frame. UE ships the Merge Actors tool plus HLOD. Godot 4 offers MeshInstance3D merging in the editor. JCE has only the lossy HLOD proxy, so a scene of many distinct props sharing one material pays one draw each.

features.feature: Per-camera clear mode decides whether the sky is drawn
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-07. All four Unity clear flags now do their own thing, on a base camera and on an overlay alike.
THE ROW'S OWN STATED BLOCKER IS GONE, TWICE OVER. It read: 'Depth Only and Nothing deliberately do NOT ship, because they are OVERLAY modes and this engine has no camera stack -- a lone camera skipping the colour clear presents an uninitialised buffer.' The first clause stopped being true when camera stacking landed (#161). The second was a REAL constraint and is the one that took work: the offscreen target's colour and D24S8 depth are created with `NULL, 0`, so keeping them on the first frame of a fresh or resized target presents uninitialised memory -- and garbage depth near the near plane rejects every draw, so the target never recovers. jce_offscreen_target_prepare_keep OVERRIDES both keeps for exactly that one frame; the bridge owns the guard because it is the only thing that knows it is new, so a caller cannot get it wrong by forgetting.
ONE ENUM, TWO QUESTIONS, TWO AUTHORITIES. jce_scene_camera_clear_draws_skybox answers the sky; the new jce_scene_camera_clear_keeps answers what survives from last frame (SKYBOX/COLOR keep nothing; DEPTH_ONLY keeps colour; NOTHING keeps both; anything out of range keeps nothing). The renderer takes two bools and knows nothing about camera modes, so the enum becomes behaviour in one file and the L4/L5 layering holds.
MEASURED, AND THE FIRST FIXTURE WAS WRONG. A still scene answers all four modes IDENTICALLY -- these modes say what survives BETWEEN frames -- so the fixture needs motion, and the first pass at reading it did not have any: the ablation (emitRate 0 vs 160) came back at 1.01% against a 0.68% floor, i.e. 'the emitter changes nothing', which would have made every number in the run a measurement of noise. Looking at the picture rather than the statistic showed the emitter rendering fine and small -- the whole-viewport summary was diluting a real effect, and the 'noise floor' was itself the particles' randomness.
Re-measured on the fountain region with a PER-MODE floor (particle emission is random, so a keep judged against a floor taken under a full clear gets credited with that randomness):
  floor  COLOR vs COLOR      mean  3.01   7.17% of px
  floor  NOTHING vs NOTHING  mean  0.55   1.85%
  signal COLOR vs NOTHING    mean 14.30  20.09%   and on an independent second pair 13.49 / 19.02%
  bright coverage of the box: 8.81% / 8.80% under a full clear, 21.24% / 21.12% under the keep -- 2.4x, reproducible to 0.12 points across runs.
The in-frame control: OUTSIDE the fountain, two runs of COLOR differ on ZERO pixels (mean 0.000), so the capture path is deterministic for static content, while COLOR vs NOTHING differs on 0.49% there -- not zero, and named rather than rounded away: it is the sphere's silhouette and its shadow edge (centroid x=731 y=650, 1389 of 3502 px inside the sphere's box), because under a kept depth the opaque geometry stops re-drawing at all.
WHY THE TWO KEEPS DIFFER SO MUCH, MECHANICALLY. DEPTH_ONLY accumulates barely (coverage 9.08% vs COLOR's 8.81%) and NOTHING accumulates hugely, which looks backwards until you read the state: opaque geometry submits with BGFX_STATE_DEPTH_TEST_LESS. Under DEPTH_ONLY the depth is cleared, so everything redraws and overwrites the kept colour; under NOTHING last frame's depth survives and the same geometry at EQUAL depth fails LESS, so nothing overwrites what accumulated. That is Unity's Don't Clear, artefacts and all, and Unity documents the same.
THE ONE LIMIT, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. A keep is honoured only through the offscreen target -- which the editor Game View always uses and the shipped exe uses when post-processing is on. Straight to the backbuffer it clears fully and LOGS why: a swapchain image is from two or three frames ago, so the mode would produce a stutter rather than a trail. Unity documents the same limitation for Don't Clear. The Inspector says this at the point of choice instead of leaving it to the log, in all 15 locales.
GUARDED. check_camera_clear_single_source.py now covers BOTH halves: each mapping function defined once, both hosts calling both, and each reaching its own sink (.draw_skybox for the sky, jce_offscreen_target_prepare_keep for the keeps). The keeps half needed the gate more than the sky half did, because its failure is INVISIBLE -- a host that stops passing them still renders a correct picture, just always the fully-cleared one. Both new arms were verified to go RED by cutting the wiring: dropping the sink and dropping the call each produced exit 1 with the right message. 10 unit cases in test_jce_camera_clear_mode.c, which drive the CARRIED clear_mode off a real resolved camera rather than a literal, so deleting the pose carry fails here too.
COMPARED: Unity clear flags (4 modes). PARITY, with the backbuffer caveat above -- which Unity shares.
features.compared: Unity clear flags (4 modes)

features.feature: Area / rect lights
features.evidence:
SHIPPED 2026-09-07.  A fourth light kind: JceAreaLight, a RECTANGLE with a width, a height and a normal.

NO LUT TEXTURES, and that is a constraint rather than a shortcut.  The reference technique is LTC (Linearly Transformed Cosines), which Unity and UE both use and which needs two more sampler stages -- fs_pbr's sixteen are FULL, a ceiling already recorded in this tree, so an LTC path could not be bound at all.  What ships is the standard analytic pair with its error named: the exact solid angle the rectangle subtends times the average of five cosines for diffuse (Frostbite's formulation), and the representative point -- the closest point ON the rectangle to the reflection ray, lit as a punctual light with the roughness widened by the angle the light subtends and the energy renormalised by (alpha/alpha')^2 -- for specular (Karis's MRP, the cheap path of every engine that ships area lights).

ONE COPY of the maths, in engine/shaders/pbr/area_light.sh, included by fs_pbr_body.sh (which is every PBR variant: default, Forward+, toon, tint, fade, texture-array) AND by fs_terrain.sc.  Those two are the only shaders that consume u_pointLights / u_spotLights, so they are the whole set a new light kind has to reach; a rect light that lit meshes and not the ground they stand on would be the shape of half-feature this ledger exists to find.

NO casts_shadow FIELD, stated at the struct rather than left to be discovered.  An area light's shadow is a soft shadow whose penumbra grows with the emitter, and this engine's local shadow atlas stores one hard depth map per light: a flag there would have produced a point light's hard shadow from a rectangle, which is a control that appears to work.  The Inspector says so beside the controls.

TWO WIRING GAPS, both found by measurement rather than by reading.  The first: sr_classify_entity caches 'is a light' in a byte the gather loop tests BEFORE it looks at any component, and that predicate named three kinds.  With the component parsing, serialising and appearing in the Inspector, the strip lit NOTHING -- and lighting the same scene with a 0.05 x 0.05 rectangle produced a byte-identical frame.  The second: reg_has_light_any is what makes the unified Light serialiser run at all, and it named the same three; test_jce_authoring_surface_sweep caught that one as 'added and then LOST by save+load'.

MEASURED (D3D11, editor scene view, envshot; a static fixture lit ONLY by the light under test -- no sun, ambient 0.02, auto-exposure off, so the light IS the signal).  Noise floor 124 px (0.012%).
  a 6.0 x 0.25 strip vs NO light ..... 606,240 px (56.59%), mean 49.27
  the same light at 0.05 x 0.05 ...... 605,989 px (56.56%), mean 42.06 from
                                       the strip -- a tight specular dot and
                                       a narrow pool, i.e. a point light,
                                       which is the correct limit
  a 2.0 x 2.0 softbox ................ 608,983 px (56.84%), mean 32.21 from
                                       the strip
The three shapes are visibly what they should be: the strip spreads the sphere's highlight into a band and the floor pool into a wide bar; the softbox gives a broad soft pool and a soft terminator.  The SHAPE reaches the pixels, which is the whole reason the feature exists and the one thing a point light cannot be dialled into.

Also here, because the feature's two uniform handles pushed the global-state detector over its baseline: the seventeen file-scope statics of the lazily-created light uniform block became one record.  global-state 859 -> 844, a net improvement of 15 while adding a light kind, and the refactor is pixel-identical (0 px differ against the pre-refactor capture).
features.compared: Unity's Rectangle area light and UE's Rect Light.  Godot has neither, so this row was behind two of three.  JCE now matches the authoring surface (rectangle, width/height, two-sided, intensity, range) and the visible behaviour (shape-carrying specular, size-softened terminator).  It does NOT match their SHADOWS -- Unity and UE both cast soft shadows from area lights and JCE casts none -- nor their LTC-exact response; both gaps are stated at the code rather than implied by the feature's presence.  Unity also has a DISC area light, which this does not.

features.feature: Light cookies (a light projects a mask)
features.evidence: NEW ROW 2026-09-17, opened by a P0 found while auditing the shader-permutation row. Cookies DID NOTHING on every desktop backend, silently. engine/shaders/pbr/fs_pbr_decl.sh declares sampler 13 as SAMPLER2D in every program this tree compiles -- the SAMPLER2DARRAY alternative beside it is behind JCE_RENDER_COOKIE_2D_ARRAY, a macro defined NOWHERE (surveyed: 12 guarded JCE_* axes in engine/shaders, that one has zero #define). jce_lighting_system.c bound a 16-layer array texture there anyway, unconditionally on BGFX_CAPS_TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY, i.e. every desktop backend -- and that texture's own TODO said its layers were never populated. All white. cookieRGB = mix(white, white, strength); radiance *= 1. The real 2D atlas never reached the shader. MEASURED on an authored fixture (tools/gen_cookie_probe_png.py, a 32px checker projected by a directional light onto a 40x40 slab; the tree had no scene that projected a cookie, which is why nobody could have seen this): noise floor 46 px at 1/255; cookie ON vs OFF **before** the fix 335 px at 1/255 -- at the floor; **after** 487,015 px (44.449%), mean 85.9, peak 216/255, and the capture shows the checker in perspective. Also 4 MB of VRAM returned on an engine whose stated baseline is 512 MB: the array texture had no writer and is gone. GATED: tools/lint/check_shader_feature_axes.py now fails on any JCE_* macro guarded in engine/shaders and defined nowhere, unless shader_axis_exempt.txt carries a reason (4/4 mutation controls, including that a name with the reason stripped stays RED). BEHIND, not parity, and the reason is the half that is still missing: the bind is SINGLE -- one cookie image per draw wins sampler 13 (spot cookies beat directional). The per-light atlas SLOT is already uploaded in u_dirLights[i*2+1].w / u_spotLights[i*4+3].y, so what remains is the array path done in ONE change: populate the layers, define the macro, bind the array. Any two of the three reproduce the defect above. || 2026-09-18 -- PARITY. Every light projects its own cookie, and getting there took FOUR halves, not three; each of the first three was correct and measured as doing nothing, because the fourth was still shared. (1) THE BLIT BLOCKER NEVER EXISTED: the removed array code's own TODO said the layers could not be filled without BGFX_TEXTURE_BLIT_SRC on each source, and bgfx asks for no such flag -- only the DESTINATION needs BGFX_TEXTURE_BLIT_DST (its own assert text, four @attention lines, and no BLIT_SRC anywhere in bgfx.cpp). The layers now fill with one blit per (slot, texture) on JCE_VIEW_MORPH_DEFORM, below every scene base so the copy lands before the colour pass that samples it. (2) THE PERMUTATION BLOCKER NEVER EXISTED EITHER, and that one was MINE: the line above saying 'texture2DArray needs GLSL 1.30+ and this engine's desktop GL shader profile is 120, so the SAMPLER2DARRAY path CANNOT COMPILE on the GL backend' was written from a stale belief that the GL floor was 2.1. The floor is GL 3.1 -- the graphics tier chain (conan/hooks/hook_bgfx_wasm_fix.py: stable 3.1 / modern 4.3 / current 4.6) has been there all along -- and bgfx REWRITES each shader's #version to 140 at that floor and emits `#define texture2DArray texture`. Profile-120 SOURCE compiles to valid GLSL 1.40. There was no permutation to write and no profile to raise: s_cookie is SAMPLER2DARRAY unconditionally, the JCE_RENDER_COOKIE_2D_ARRAY guard is deleted, and the exemption that recorded the wrong claim is retired in tools/lint/shader_axis_exempt.txt with both corrections written down. (3) SLOT AND STRENGTH ARE PER LIGHT: the atlas slot rides in u_spotLights[i*4+3].y / u_dirLights[i*2+1].w and the strength in .z, so the gate is 'does this light have a cookie' rather than 'is this light the one that won the sampler'. The dead array code had read u_cookieParams.x (the has-cookie flag) as the spot slice and u_cookieDirParams.w (packed as literal 0) as the directional one -- two more wrong fields that only a compiled reader could expose. (4) THE PROJECTION WAS SHARED TOO, and this is what kept the fixture blank after the other three were right: u_cookieSpotVP was ONE mat4 built from whichever light won the single bind, so every other cookie-bearing light projected through the FIRST light's frustum, landed outside [0,1] and was masked to white -- indistinguishable from a light with no cookie. fs_pbr_main.sh now DERIVES each light's frustum from its own position/direction/cone, reproducing jce_m4_perspective(2*acos(outerCos),1,..)*jce_m4_look_at() term for term, so per-light projection costs no uniform at all and the shared mat4 upload is gone. HOW THE FOURTH WAS FOUND: the two-cookie fixture put a checker on the left light and stripes on the right, and the two textures' bgfx handles SWAPPED between two runs (21/0 then 0/21) while the picture did not -- the pattern followed the LIGHT, never the texture. That is what ruled out the texture and named the matrix. MEASURED (caged_kingdom/resources/assets/scenes/cookie_two_probe.scene.json, two spot lights, two different masks, d3d11, frame 300): noise floor 0 px over two runs of the same build. Left pool, clear of the cone overlap: shared matrix vs derived per-light = 1,113 px (0.268%), mean 0.0071, peak 61 -- edge rounding only, which is the POSITIVE CONTROL that the derivation reproduces the matrix for the light that already worked. Right pool over the same change: 140,782 px (33.771%), mean 78.9, peak 251 -- blank to striped. ABLATION JCE_COOKIE_NO_ARRAY=1 (cookies off, same scene, no edit): left 33.688%, right 33.771% -- symmetric, so both lights really carry one. TWO MORE DEFECTS OF THE SAME FAMILY, both from bgfx handle 0 being VALID: the cookie atlas used 0 as its empty-slot sentinel (a cookie that legitimately got handle 0 was assigned a slot and then skipped by the layer sync), and the time-of-day sun in jce_sr_draw.c was memset, so its zeroed cookie_texture registered a stranger's texture into a slot. The sentinels are now JCE_COOKIE_SLOT_EMPTY/_RESERVED (0xFFFE/0xFFFF) and the header gained jce_dir_light_desc_default() / jce_spot_light_desc_default(), because a comment saying 'JCE_TEXTURE_INVALID = disabled' cannot defend a field whose memset default is a valid handle. THE 2D FALLBACK IS GONE: s_cookie is an array sampler, so binding a plain 2D texture there is a TYPE mismatch that desktop tolerates and WebGL2 rejects for the whole draw; when the caps bit is absent the bind is a 1x1 white ONE-LAYER array and every slot is forced to 0, so cookies switch off cleanly. u_cookieParams became u_iesParams (.x has_ies, .y ies_spot_index) -- and its old .w was `cookie_spot >= 0 ? cookie_spot : ies_spot`, so a scene with a cookie on one light and an IES profile on another applied the IES curve to the light holding the COOKIE. CLOSES the candidate row render.lights.cookie-multiple-per-frame, which is removed from contracts/engine-parity-candidates.json: it described this same single-bind limit, and two of the three wrong slice expressions it named (u_cookieParams.x for the spot slice, u_cookieDirParams.w for the directional one) were exactly right.
features.compared: Unity gives every light its own cookie (2D for spot/directional, cube for point) with no per-draw contention; UE has light functions per light; Godot 4 has per-light projector textures. JCE now projects a different cookie from every spot light in one draw, up to JCE_COOKIE_ATLAS_CAPACITY (16) distinct masks with LRU eviction beyond that. Still behind on POINT-light cookies, which need a cube atlas -- tracked separately, not by this row.

features.feature: A light illuminates only chosen object layers
features.evidence:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-08. Rendering layers now work under Forward+ as well as forward, which is what this row was short of.
WHAT WAS WRONG WAS ALSO EXPENSIVE. Forward+ was REFUSED for any frame whose light environment carried a mask, because the clustered shader reads point and spot parameters out of s_cluster, built once per frame with no receiver in sight -- so a CPU-side mask could not reach them, and masking the directionals while silently not masking the locals is the half-working shape this feature was reverted for once already. Correct, and a performance cliff: authoring ONE light layer cost the whole clustered path, on exactly the hardware clustered lighting exists for.
THE ROUTE WAS THE ONE THIS ROW WROTE DOWN, taken unchanged. Each cluster light's mask rides in the two SPARE lanes of its L3 texel (which held 0,0), split into 16-bit halves because a 32-bit mask does not survive a float: 2^31 needs a 32-bit mantissa and there are 24. The receiver's layer rides in u_areaParams.y -- a vec4 with three spare lanes that the per-draw light upload already carries, so no new uniform and no second cluster build. The test is mod(floor(m / exp2(b)), 2), the only form that survives the GLSL 1.20 floor the OpenGL backend compiles at: it has no integer bitwise operators at all.
SET ON BOTH EXITS of jce_light_env_apply_for_layer, including the unmasked fast path -- the cluster carries masks whether or not the CPU-side packs do, so a frame with no masked light still has to say which layer is receiving or the clustered path reads whatever was in that lane last.
MEASURED IN PLAY (the runtime-parity surface), two spheres differing in NOTHING but their layer, lit by one masked POINT light -- the previous light-layer fixture used a directional, which never enters the cluster and so could not have caught anything here:
  the mask under Forward+     69073 px (6.30%), mean 10.325, peak 184
  the same under forward      69073 px (6.30%), mean 10.325, peak 184
  masked Forward+ vs masked forward     IDENTICAL -- not one pixel differs
  unmasked Forward+ vs unmasked forward IDENTICAL -- not one pixel differs
Two different lighting code paths agreeing to the byte, masked and unmasked, is the parity claim itself: the cluster loop reproduces the brute-force formula exactly, which is what its comments promise.
THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS, because 'both pictures agree' would ALSO be true if Forward+ had quietly stayed off: with the old refusal restored, the same masked scene asking for Forward+ reports active=0; with the fix, active=1. Same scene, same request, opposite outcome -- and the picture byte-identical either way, so the cliff is removed at no visual cost. Forward+ being genuinely engaged was confirmed from the renderer's own decision, not inferred from the pixels.
A SEPARATE FINDING, RECORDED RATHER THAN FOLDED IN: the editor's SCENE view does not call jce_light_env_apply_for_layer at all, so per-receiver light layers do not apply there -- the first four captures of this measurement were taken there and showed the mask doing nothing, which is what sent the investigation to Play. The Scene view is a viewing aid rather than the game, and the Game View and the shipped exe both take the path that works, but it is a real editor/runtime divergence and it is written down here instead of being left as a surprise.
SCOPE, unchanged from the forward path and stated rather than left to be found: the mask drops a light's DIRECT term -- diffuse, specular and its shadow go together -- and touches neither ambient, baked probes nor volumetric fog, none of which have a receiver. features.feature: Planar reflections
features.evidence:
Mirror the camera through the water plane, render the scene from there into an offscreen target, sample it back projectively and blend by Schlick's Fresnel over water's F0. engine/src/renderer/jce_planar_reflection.c + the JceWaterComponent fields planar_reflection / planar_intensity, wired at BOTH editor viewports and jce_default_main. MEASURED: red and green pillars over a 40x40 lake, D3D11, envshot, two captures of the same build as the noise floor (1947 px / 0.182%, peak 1/255). Planar reflection on vs off changes 503083 px (46.96%), mean 6.584, peak 39/255 -- and the bounding control says that is the RIGHT extent: deleting the lake entity changes 503468 px (46.99%), so the reflection touches essentially every water pixel and nothing else. The capture shows both pillars mirrored below their bases in their own colours, with the sky across the whole surface. TWO LIMITS, both forced by measurement, both in the header: (1) ONE FRAME LATE. bgfx runs views in ascending id order and the water draws in the scene's COLOUR view at base+0, so no base-relative id can render before its consumer; the reflection takes the reclaimed absolute band at 238 and is sampled next frame. (2) WATER, NOT ARBITRARY SURFACES. fs_pbr declares sixteen samplers in slots 0..15 with NONE free -- measured with `jce.py shader-inspect`, the tool landed two commits earlier -- against bgfx's ceiling of 16. fs_water has seven free. A general mirror material needs its own shader. BEHIND rather than parity for that second reason: Unity's Planar Reflection Probe and Unreal's Planar Reflection apply to any surface, this applies to water. THREE DEFECTS FOUND GETTING HERE, only one of them this feature's own: bgfx_set_view_order overwrites the CONTIGUOUS window [first, first+count), so a second render from a high base wrapped over the ids the main render had just claimed and the viewport composited a BLANK frame (caught by the capture harness's own blank-frame guard, isolated by ablating that one call); JceSceneRenderConfig::reduced_pass had to exist because a second render otherwise refills sr->ssao_depth_tex and sr->ssao_normal_tex, which the MAIN view owns; and bgfx handle 0 is a VALID handle, so three calloc'd uniform handles passed BGFX_HANDLE_IS_VALID, were never created, and every set went to whoever owns handle 0 -- three probes and a forced-constant test to find, in the same session that had documented that exact hazard in jce_fs_target_init hours earlier.

2026-09-20 -- PARITY. It applies to any surface now, which was the one reason this row said behind.

WHAT CHANGED. JceReflectionProbeComponent gains a PLANAR mode (Unity's Planar Reflection Probe, Unreal's Planar Reflection actor) with a world plane normal and two tolerances, and the reflection is composited in SCREEN SPACE rather than sampled from a material shader. The composite reads the depth buffer and the SSR G-buffer normal -- whose alpha already carries roughness -- reconstructs each pixel's world position, and blends premultiplied 'over', the same state the SSR composite uses and at the same view id, submitted second so the accurate reflection wins over the screen-space guess. Three tests decide whether a pixel is the mirror: on the plane within a tolerance, facing the same way within an angle, inside the probe's influence box with a faded edge. That is why a polished floor, a wet road and a still lake all get it and none of them needed a shader written for them -- fs_pbr still has no seventeenth sampler slot and no longer needs one.

MEASURED, D3D11, envshot, a polished floor with two coloured pillars and a wall standing on it. NOISE FLOOR: two captures of the same build, 0 px. SUBJECT: probe on vs no probe, 623581 px (56.913%), mean 10.699, peak 165. The capture shows both pillars mirrored beneath their bases in their own colours, the wall continuing below its foot, and sky across the rest of the floor.

FOUR CONTROLS, because above the noise floor says something changed, not that it was the thing intended:
  SAME ENTITY IN A CUBE MODE: 0 px. The effect is the mode, not one more entity in the scene.
  PROBE BOX SHRUNK TO EXCLUDE THE CAMERA: 0 px. The influence volume is load-bearing.
  MATTE FLOOR (roughness 1.0), probe vs no probe: 59 px at peak 1, against 623581 at peak 165 on the polished one. The roughness fade is load-bearing -- and the FIRST version of this control was wrong: it compared a matte floor WITH a probe against a polished floor WITHOUT one, moved two variables, and read 56.8%.
  NORMAL TEST RELAXED to 89 degrees with an 8 m tolerance: 1410 px more (peak 87), all on the wall's base. Without that test a wall standing on the floor takes the floor's reflection, which reads as a lighting bug.

FOUR DEFECTS FOUND GETTING HERE, and every one of them looked like 'the effect is weak' rather than like a bug:
  NO VIEW RECT. The composite shares its bgfx view id with the SSR composite and never set the rect, so it inherited whatever the last user of that id left -- correct in every frame SSR also ran, and drawing into a stale rect in the rest. Before: 59 px at peak 1. After: 71556 px at peak 161.
  A MATRIX MAINTAINED BY SOMEONE ELSE'S FEATURE. The composite read sr->cur_view_proj, which is only written when TAA velocity is on; with r.taa=0 it holds an earlier frame's camera, so every pixel reconstructed to a warped world position. The symptom was a mirror on a thin band of distant floor and nowhere else, because only there did the stale matrix land within the on-plane tolerance. A per-pixel diagnostic that coloured each pixel by WHICH test rejected it is what showed the near floor being refused as off-plane.
  THE WRONG ASPECT RATIO. The mirrored render used its target's aspect (640x360, 1.778) and the viewport that samples it was 1.521. Logging both matrices showed the mirror's view-projection was the main one composed with the plane reflection -- correct to four decimals in y -- with its x row scaled by exactly 1.521/1.778, so every projective lookup landed 14% toward the centre.
  THE MIRROR REFLECTED ITS OWN GLASS. With an ordinary projection the mirrored camera sits below the plane looking up, and the first thing in front of it is the underside of the surface it is a mirror for. On a 0.2 m floor slab that filled three quarters of the target with an unlit black field. Oblique near-plane clipping (Lengyel) now makes the near plane the mirror plane. A/B of that one change: 56.908% of the frame, mean 90.449. Displaying the whole reflection target rather than the strip the composite happened to sample is what found it -- the first two readings were of the bottom half of a target whose geometry was all in the top half.

AND IT CHANGED A SHIPPED FEATURE. Water's planar reflection now routes through the same code and therefore gained the oblique clip it never had: a lake no longer reflects its own bed. Measured on hidden_cove, clip on vs off: 408071 px (37.244%), mean 1.002, peak 18 -- real, small, and physically the right direction. Water itself still works: planar on vs off is 95.684% at mean 30.265 against that scene's noise floor of peak 5.

ONE LIMIT, STATED: one planar probe is live per frame -- the nearest whose influence box contains the camera -- because a second probe is a second full scene render. The inspector says so rather than leaving a silent probe. The one-frame lateness from the original row still holds and for the same reason.

THE PRE-PASS GATE GAINED A SIXTH REQUESTER, and that is the half-wired shape this ledger exists to catch: the composite needs the depth and G-buffer normal that pass produces, so without it the probe draws nothing -- and a probe that draws nothing is indistinguishable from a probe out of range. It would have worked in every scene that happened to have SSR on. tests/middleware/scene/test_jce_sr_depth_prepass_gate.c asserts both halves.
features.compared: Unity's Planar Reflection Probe (HDRP) and Unreal's Planar Reflection actor, both of which apply to any surface and render in the same frame; Godot 4 has no planar reflection at all. This one is water-only (fs_pbr has no free sampler slot, measured) and one frame late (no base-relative view id can precede the colour pass that samples it).

features.evidence:

I listed every shader under engine/shaders (51 files) and postfx/ contains bloom, chromatic, composite, fxaa, grayscale, motion_vec, present, rcas, reveal_dissolve, taa, tonemap, tsr, underwater, vignette and nothing else. Searching engine/, editor/, scripts/, tools/ and scripting/ for depth_of_field, depthoffield, bokeh, coc, circle of confusion, focus_distance, aperture and f_stop returns exactly one line — a comment at jce_scene.h:1377 naming depth of field as one of the passes that would read water depth if it existed. There is also no focus/aperture field on JceCamera (jce_camera.h has target and fov, no lens model).  || REFUTATION ATTEMPTED 2026-09-06 and FAILED to find an implementation: grep across engine/include, engine/src, editor/src, engine/shaders and tools for depth_of_field / depthOfField / bokeh / focal_dist / focus_distance / aperture returns ZERO first-party hits. Not a truncated-grep verdict -- the search covered six spellings and every tree that could hold one. The claim stands: absent.  || CLOSED 2026-09-06. Rack focus on JceSceneRenderingSettings (dof_enabled, focus distance, focus range, max blur radius), pushed per frame by jce_scene_renderer.c and gathered inside the existing uber composite -- a 16-tap golden-angle disk weighted by each SAMPLE's own CoC, so a sharp foreground pixel cannot bleed into a blurred background one.
NOT an entry in JcePostFXType: that enum ends in a COUNT that sizes public arrays (JceSceneRenderingSettings.postfx_enabled among them), so growing it to add an effect moves every member after it -- a real ABI break. Motion blur set the same precedent for the same reason.
THE SHADER HAS NO PER-BACKEND BRANCH, and that was the design decision. It never linearises depth: the four depth edges are projected on the CPU through the same matrix that filled the buffer, and handed over SORTED numerically rather than named near/far. Which numeric end is nearer depends on reverse-Z and on GL's [-1,1] clip range against D3D's [0,1]; being OUTSIDE the in-focus band does not. This renderer has shipped twelve mirrored per-backend branches in a single campaign, so the one that does not have to exist should not.
MEASURED (d3d11, hidden_cove/beauty, frame 300, max CoC 0.02):
  floor                        5336 px (0.498%)  mean 0.003
  off vs on, focus 30 m      818497 px (76.40%)  mean 7.874   153x floor
  focus 30 m vs 200 m        121890 px (11.38%)  mean 1.112

The panel reads jce_postfx_get_depth_of_field_active and says so when the effect is switched on but has no depth buffer to work from -- 'is it on' and 'is it doing anything' are different questions, and every unwired-feature defect in this engine lived in the gap between them.
features.compared: Unity URP ships a Depth Of Field volume override with Gaussian and Bokeh modes; HDRP adds a physical camera with aperture and focus distance. UE's post-process volume has Gaussian, Cinematic (diaphragm) and mobile DOF driven by focal distance and f-stop. Godot 4 has CameraAttributesPractical/Physical with DOF blur near/far and focus distance. A JCE game cannot rack focus at all, and there is no public API a script could reach for. JCE now has focus distance, focus range and a blur-radius cap, authored on the scene. No physical camera (f-stop, focal length) and no bokeh shape: the gather is a uniform disk.

features.feature: Motion blur
features.evidence: IMPLEMENTED. It was the audit's signature shape in its purest form: JceRenderPipelineDesc.enable_motion_blur set by three editor UIs, serialised to .rp.json, defaulted ON by the ULTRA preset, cooked into the shipped PAK, answered by jce_render_pipeline_feature_enabled("motion_blur") -- and read by no render pass, with the field's own comment saying so. It now runs INSIDE the composite pass (no extra view, no extra target): 8 taps back along the per-pixel velocity, on the HDR colour before the bloom add and the tonemap, so a smeared highlight blooms as a streak. Trail length is JceRenderPipelineDesc.motion_blur_intensity, appended, with 0 resolving to the engine default in ONE accessor -- every .rp.json in existence predates that key, and a direct field read would render unblurred while the toggle said ON (4 unit cases; the control that drops the rule fails 2 of them by name). The camera reprojection matrices moved OUT of the TAA gate in jce_scene_renderer_taa_begin_frame, because they are camera state and TAA was only their first consumer; taa_end_frame now records the previous camera unconditionally, so "previous" means the previous frame instead of whenever TAA was last on. GPU EVIDENCE (D3D11, 1280x837, hidden_cove, frame 300, camera spinning 1.5 deg/frame): noise floor of two captures of the same build = 0.379% of pixels, >4 0.00%, >16 0.00%. off -> on = mean 4.393, 72.0% of pixels, >4 26.8%, >16 9.78%, and image std falls 46.17 -> 44.98 (a blur reduces variance, which is the right direction). CONTROL, the same build with a STILL camera: 0.83% of pixels, >4 0.02%, >16 0.01%, std unchanged at 55.69 -- at the floor, so the pass costs a static frame nothing. TWO DEFECTS THE GPU RUN FOUND AND THE UNIT TESTS COULD NOT. (1) The first working version blurred along the renderer's per-object velocity G-buffer, which measures |delta| ~ 6e-5 NDC (0.08 px) under that spin -- its previous view-proj is this frame's -- so the frame came back AT THE NOISE FLOOR while every C-side probe said active=1. The camera-only reprojection is used instead, and the velocity buffer's own gap is recorded rather than papered over: it is TAA's problem too. (2) The sub-pixel no-op threshold was a bare 1e-4, which is 0.13 px at 1280 and 0.05 px at 3840; a STATIC frame moved 33.3% of its pixels and lost image std. It is now half a texel, passed in from the CPU.
features.compared: Unity URP/HDRP Motion Blur volume override (camera-only in URP, per-object in HDRP); UE Motion Blur post-process settings; Godot 4 CameraAttributes has none, so this is ahead of Godot. At parity with URP: same camera-only source, same intensity knob. Behind HDRP and UE on per-OBJECT motion -- an object crossing a still frame is not blurred, because the velocity buffer that would express it does not currently carry motion (see the evidence above); the pass is already written against s_texMotion, so fixing that buffer switches this on without touching the blur.

features.feature: Shadow bias means the same distance in every cascade
features.evidence: OPENED 2026-09-19 BY THE CASCADE NEAR-PLANE WORK (85de58ad), and opened as its own row rather than folded into that fix, because it is not the defect that fix repairs and calling the fix complete would have hidden it. THE DEPTH BIAS IS A NORMALIZED-DEPTH CONSTANT. csm_shadow.sh and fs_pbr_decl.sh both compute `depth_bias = inv_map_size * mix(..) * bias_scale * (1 + slope*4)` and compare it against a shadow-map sample, so its WORLD meaning is that number times the cascade's ortho depth range -- a quantity nothing in the expression accounts for. jce_csm.h already exports depth_range[] for exactly this class of reason, and today only the PCSS penumbra reads it. MEASURED, one frame, camera at 1.8 m, scene 12 m tall: shadow_far 300 gives depth ranges 83 / 154 / 285 / 800-ish across the four cascades, so the same bias number is 11x the world offset in cascade 3 that it is in cascade 0 -- nobody chose that ratio, it is the fit's geometry leaking into a tuning constant. It also moves with the PROJECT: at shadow_far 300 cascade 0's world depth bias is 89 mm and at shadow_far 40 it is 20 mm, so shortening the shadow distance for performance silently retunes every shadow in the game. AND IT IS WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX FOR THE NEAR-PLANE HOLE WAS REJECTED: pushing the near plane out far enough (a closed form, provably sufficient, all 48 measured configurations to zero) deepened depth_range and the rendered shadow area went DOWN 2-3.6% at every yaw -- on flat ground under a 12-degree sun the ground displacement went from 1.29 m to 3.75 m. The geometry could not be corrected because a tuning constant was pinned to it. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a world-referenced bias -- `depth_bias = BIAS_TEXELS * texel_world(c) / depth_range(c) * (1 + slope*4)` -- which needs one new per-cascade vec4 uniform (texel_world/depth_range), its upload, and the two sampling sites that compute a depth bias (csm_shadow.sh:177 for terrain and water, fs_pbr_decl.sh:571 for meshes). NOT DONE HERE because it changes shadow contact on every surface in every scene and its oracle is an acne-vs-peter-panning sweep, which is its own measurement and not a rider on a bug fix. The separate normal-offset term (u_csmParams.z * bias_scale) is already a world distance and is not at issue. || 2026-09-19 -- CLOSED. The bias is now a number of SHADOW TEXELS of world offset, converted to normalised depth by the cascade's own scale: engine/shaders/pbr/shadow_bias.sh, called from the two sites that compute a cascade depth bias (csm_shadow.sh for terrain and water, fs_pbr_decl.sh for meshes). NO NEW UNIFORM WAS NEEDED and that is the whole reason this was cheap: u_csmPenumbra already carried the bridge -- per-cascade depth-range units per shadow texel, uploaded every frame since the contact-hardening search was written -- so the number the engine had to know was already being told to the shader and exactly one consumer was listening. CALIBRATED, NOT GUESSED: matching cascade 0's old behaviour exactly gives texels = depth_range(0)/(2*radius(0)), which over shadow distances 40..600 m and sun elevations 12..45 deg lands in 1.35..2.09 and clusters at 1.6. So 1.6 texels for terrain and water, 4.8 for meshes (their historical 3x, kept rather than silently removed), and cascade 0 stays within +/-15% of what it rendered before. What goes is the mix(1,2,cascade) / mix(3,6,cascade) ladders and the mix(0.01,0.08,cascade) ceiling, all three of which existed to compensate one constant at a time for a bias whose world meaning was the cascade fit's geometry -- the ceiling's own comment said so: 'the much larger world depth range it represents'. MEASURED on a fixture whose posts' CONTACT POINTS are on screen, eye pinned, TAA off, noise floor 0 px in both bands: sun 35 deg, near band 1285-1574 px darker and 0 lighter, far band 1269-1310 px darker and 0 lighter; at a grazing 7 deg sun, 682 near and 2235 far, again 0 lighter anywhere. ZERO PIXELS LIGHTER IS THE VERDICT: a smaller bias can only add shadow, so a single lighter pixel would have meant something else changed. The far band moves 2x as densely as the near one, which is the prediction written down before the numbers were read -- its bias was the one that was wrong. NO ACNE: the changed pixels are 79% / 51% four-neighbour coherent and the diff is connected stripes, not texel-frequency speckle; the grazing-sun run is the case acne lives in and it is the one with the most restored shadow and still no speckle. A FIXTURE THAT COULD NOT SEE IT, RECORDED BECAUSE IT LOOKED LIKE A RESULT: the first acne check came back bit-identical, and a positive control explained why -- setting the mesh bias to 0.0 was ALSO bit-identical, while 0.5 moved 23643 px. That scene's casters stood behind the camera, so only the far parts of their shadows were visible and the depth gap there is far larger than any bias. PETER-PANNING IS A CONTACT PHENOMENON; a fixture whose contact points are off screen cannot measure it, and 'no change' from one reads exactly like 'no effect'. GATES: tools/lint/check_shadow_bias_units.py (5 of 5 mutations red, baseline green -- either site reverting to the inv_map_size form, the call surviving only as a comment, the bridge replaced by a constant, and the named site list matching nothing) and tests/renderer/test_jce_csm_bias_units.c, which checks the bridge is depth-range-per-texel exactly and then measures the defect it replaced so the assertions cannot be vacuous: a fixed normalised bias spans 10.4x between cascade 0 and 3, and 4.8x on cascade 0 alone between shadow_far 300 and 40.
features.compared: Unity exposes shadow bias and normal bias per light in WORLD units and scales them by the cascade's texel size, so the same setting means the same distance in every cascade and does not move when Shadow Distance changes; UE's slope-scaled depth bias is likewise applied in world space per cascade. JCE's number is in normalized shadow-map depth, so its physical meaning is whatever the cascade fit happened to produce. JCE now expresses it in shadow texels of world offset, per cascade, which is the quantity acne is actually a function of -- the depth gradient across one texel -- so the same authored number means the same thing in every cascade and at every shadow distance.

features.feature: Screen-space global illumination
features.evidence: One diffuse bounce, screen space. engine/src/renderer/jce_ssgi.c + engine/shaders/ssgi/, deliberately the same shape as jce_ssr.c: it takes the lit colour, the depth pre-pass depth and its NORMAL target, marches short rays through the depth buffer, and hands back an RT the scene renderer ADDS onto the scene colour before postfx. Wired at both composite call sites -- editor viewport and jce_default_main -- at the same view offset, so Play and the shipped exe cannot diverge. Scene settings (ssgi / ssgiIntensity / ssgiRadius) round-trip; JceRenderPipelineDesc.enable_ssgi is off in every preset except ULTRA and exposed in both editor pipeline surfaces; 6 i18n keys x 15 locales. MEASURED on a red pillar over a grey floor, D3D11, envshot, two captures of the same build as the noise floor (30 px / 0.003%, peak 1/255): SSGI on vs off changes 100988 px (9.43%), mean 0.164, peak 13/255, and the written diff image puts the change exactly where a bounce belongs -- the pillar's shadowed faces and a halo on the floor at its base, fading with distance. NEGATIVE CONTROL, and a tight one: collapsing ssgiRadius to 0.001 leaves every other cost and code path identical -- same gate, same depth+normal pre-pass, same RT, same composite -- and lands EXACTLY on the noise floor against the OFF render: 30 px, the same 30 px two captures of one build differ by. BEHIND, not parity, and the gap is named: (1) NO DENOISER -- four rays per pixel is a grainy estimator, and Unity's SSGI, UE's Lumen screen traces and Godot's SSIL are all denoised; (2) NO ALBEDO G-BUFFER -- this renderer's normal target carries rgb=normal, a=roughness and nothing else, so the receiver's own lit colour stands in for its albedo, which over-counts on brightly lit surfaces. Both are subsystem work, not a knob. The ray pattern is a pure function of gl_FragCoord (no frame counter): two runs of a frame are byte-identical, which is what this tree's capture harness compares -- a temporally rotated pattern would look better under TAA and make every A/B here meaningless. Loop bounds are compiled in at 4 rays x 8 steps: at 8x16 fxc ground for minutes per backend and the unrolled body would have issued up to 384 texture fetches per pixel, against a stated integrated-GPU baseline.  ||  2026-09-08 -- THE DENOISER LANDED, AND THIS ROW'S OWN NUMBERS ABOVE WERE MEASURED ON A FIXTURE THE CAMERA NEVER CONTAINED. Both halves belong here, and the second one first because it is why the first was possible to get wrong. THE CORRECTION: the 'red pillar over a grey floor' fixture cited above was authored with a `contract` block of its own invention ({"format_version": 1}) instead of the tree's ({"name": "jce.scene", "major": 1, "minor": 0}), so the loader reported '4 entities' and drew NONE of them, and the orbit camera used a NEGATIVE pitch, which in tools/envshot.py's rig puts the eye BELOW the target looking up (every preset that looks down is positive: forest 42, canopy 38, slope 32). The captures were of sky and the editor grid. A re-run against them therefore produced 53 px at peak 1/255 and I read that as 'the effect does not reproduce', wrote three shader diagnostics and a denoiser, and reverted the denoiser as unvalidatable. The guard that names exactly this (assert_subject_in_frame) existed the whole time and did not run, because it reads the engine's stdout and tools/envshot.py only kept stdout when --log was passed -- it printed 'subject-in-frame NOT verified (pass --log)' on every capture instead. FIXED AT THE INSTRUMENT: --log now defaults to build/envshots/<name>.log, so both guards run on every capture and a missing log is a hard error rather than a skipped check; verified by re-running a camera aimed at empty space with no --log, which now exits on 'visible=0 of total=0'. THE MEASUREMENT, on a fixture whose subject is verified in frame (2 visible entities, D3D11, a 12 x 6 m lit red wall standing on a 24 x 24 m grey floor -- a Cornell-style colour-bleed setup, nothing animated, fog, bloom, tonemap, vignette, SSAO, SSR and IBL all off): SSGI on vs off changes 155015 px (9.13% of envshot's viewport region), mean 2.11, peak 68/255, and the signed change is RED-dominant (R +22.9 vs G +6.3, B +6.3) -- the wall's colour on the floor, which is the thing the effect is for. NOISE FLOOR, two captures of one build: 2432 px (0.14%), peak 1/255. THE FILTER: the composite is now a joint bilateral 3x3 gather at a 2-texel stride, guided by the same depth and normal target the march was handed (remembered on the module so jce_ssgi_composite keeps its two-argument signature and the editor viewport and jce_default_main cannot pass it different inputs). It is IN the composite because SSGI owns exactly two base-relative view ids -- 26 march, 27 composite -- and 28/29 are the fullscreen fold-back and the editor overlay, so a third pass would have to displace one of them. VALIDATED as a denoiser and not merely as a change: on the isolated bounce (on - off), restricted to the pixels where the UNFILTERED build has one so the filtered build is judged on the same footprint, mean |Laplacian| of luminance falls from 20.114 to 4.781 -- 23.8% of it, 944x the run-to-run floor of that same quantity (0.0162) -- while the bounce LEVEL keeps 96.9% (11.88 -> 11.51). The third number is what stops the first two: a filter that dimmed the bounce away would also drop the high frequencies and would be strictly worse. Spill is the filter's own support and no more: of 80352 pixels newly lit outside the unfiltered footprint, 79927 (99.47%) lie within its +-2 px reach and the remaining 425 are all exactly 1/255, below the 2432-px noise floor. HIT COVERAGE (the RT's alpha) is deliberately NOT a weight -- bounce.rgb is already normalised by rays CAST, so weighting by rays that HIT is a positive bias; an earlier version that did it RAISED the bounce's high-frequency energy by 37.6%. GATED by tools/lint/check_ssgi_denoise_guided.py: the shader must sample s_depth and s_normal at TWO distinct coordinates (centre and tap), jce_ssgi_composite() must bind sampler stages 1 and 2, and the composite must not read the RT's alpha. All five mutations verified to turn it red, and the first rule was REWRITTEN because of one of them: 'samples s_depth somewhere' passed with the per-tap fetch deleted, since the centre fetch remained -- i.e. it passed on a filter that had become a plain blur. THREE DEFECTS FOUND WHILE READING, all fixed in the same change: sr->ssgi_active_frame was the one flag missing from the per-frame reset block, so a frame that wanted SSGI and failed to create it kept last frame's true and composited an RT nothing had written; jce_scene_renderer.c and jce_editor_viewport_common.h both still documented SSGI as living at base+64/65, four commits after it moved to 26/27; and fs_ssgi.sc's header named u_ssgi_params1.w 'max_bounce', a parameter written as a literal 0.0 and read by nothing. STILL BEHIND, and now for one reason instead of two: there is no ALBEDO G-BUFFER, so the receiver's own lit colour stands in for its albedo and over-counts on brightly lit surfaces. The denoise is SPATIAL ONLY -- Unity's SSGI and UE's Lumen also accumulate temporally, which this cannot do while the ray pattern stays a pure function of gl_FragCoord, and that determinism is what every A/B in this repository is compared with. || 2026-09-18 -- THE ALBEDO G-BUFFER LANDED, the second of the two named gaps (the denoiser was the first). The depth pre-pass now writes the material's base-colour FACTOR into attachment 1 and fs_ssgi.sc reads it as the receiver's albedo, where it had been reading the receiver's LIT COLOUR -- which contains the direct lighting and therefore counted it twice. || ATTACHMENT 1, FIXED, and velocity moved to 2 for it. Allocating albedo only when SSGI is on would shift velocity's index, and the fragment shaders write FIXED gl_FragData indices -- so on the frames SSGI was off, albedo would land in the VELOCITY target and TAA would ghost with nothing in the TAA code to explain it. The alternative is a shader variant per combination, which is what a keyword system would generate and this engine does not have one (see shaders.keywords.static-permutations). Cost stated rather than hidden: one RGBA8 at full res, 8.3 MB at 1080p, allocated whether SSGI is on or not. || MEASURED on an authored fixture (a saturated wall bouncing onto a NEUTRAL floor -- the one case where the two receiver terms differ visibly): noise floor 29 px at 1/255; SSGI on vs off 163,062 px (14.88%), mean 3.009, peak 102; albedo target vs lit-colour receiver (JCE_SSGI_NO_ALBEDO=1 as the ablation) 157,638 px (14.39%), mean 2.621, peak 91. The ablation is nearly as large as the whole pass, which is what 'the receiver term dominated the result' predicts. || AND THE DIRECTION IS THE PHYSICS, not just a magnitude: over the pixels that changed, mean RGB goes 202.0/104.5/93.1 (lit colour) -> 202.8/129.9/121.7 (albedo). G +25.3 and B +28.7 against R +0.8 -- the red bounce was being applied a SECOND time by the receiver term, and removing it lets green and blue back. A uniform brightness shift would have been the signature of a scale error; a chromatic one is the signature of the double-count this row named. || THREE INDEPENDENT GATES, found the hard way and recorded so the next person does not: the pass is inert unless the SCENE's own `ssgi` flag, the RENDER PIPELINE's ssgi feature, and a non-zero ssgiIntensity/ssgiRadius are all set. Setting only the pipeline one produced a capture IDENTICAL to SSGI off -- which reads exactly like the feature being broken, and is why the on/off control is measured every time rather than assumed. || ONE COARSENESS, stated: the albedo is the material's base-colour FACTOR, not its texture. Binding every material's albedo map in a pre-pass that binds nothing today would make the pre-pass as state-heavy as the colour pass, on a stated integrated-GPU baseline, to refine a term that is already a screen-space estimate. And the instanced velocity batch binds WHITE, because its batch key carries quantised roughness and nothing else -- a neutral error, not the wrong one it replaces.
features.compared: Unity HDRP/URP screen-space global illumination (denoised, with a ray-traced mode); Unreal's Lumen screen traces; Godot 4's SSIL. features.feature: A shipped game with no post-processing renders its scene
features.evidence: FOUND AND FIXED 2026-09-08 while trying to photograph a shipped build. The runtime's offscreen postfx bridge is created at JCE_VIEW_RUNTIME_GAME -- the same view id its direct-to-backbuffer fallback renders into -- and jce_offscreen_target_prepare_keep bound that view's framebuffer to the offscreen target BEFORE the code asked whether any post effect was enabled. When none was, the bridge declined to present and the fallback drew the entire game into a target nobody shows. Every shipped project with no post-processing rendered a black window. MEASURED on one two-sphere scene, same frame, same camera: avg_lum 217.4 with one postfx effect enabled, 0.0 with none -- and with none, exactly ONE lit pixel at (0,0) holding the sky colour, because an unset bgfx view rect clamps to 1x1. TWO FIXES, both of the class rather than the instance: jce_renderer_begin_frame_3d now binds the backbuffer to the view it is handed (that is what the function means -- draw this view TO THE WINDOW -- and a bgfx framebuffer binding is sticky), and the bridge now decides whether it is needed BEFORE it claims any view. jce_accept.py's screenshot stage -- the gate that asks whether the SHIPPED artifact renders -- went from FAIL ('the sampled 3D area is uniform') to PASS, 6 PASS / 0 FAIL. It could not have passed for any project on this path, and its sibling DIAG line in jce_renderer_bgfx_callback.c ('root-cause hunt for F12/F9 black') had been recording the symptom without the cause.

features.evidence: Seven backends -- Lua, Python, C, C++, C#, Java, JS -- all exercised by jce.py smoke on every SDK build, with a cross-language differential test. Unity ships C#; UE ships C++ and Blueprints; Godot ships GDScript and C#. AND THE SHIPPED ARTEFACT NOW HAS TO CARRY THEM: every backend bar Lua detects its own toolchain and switches itself OFF when it is absent -- right for a contributor, wrong for the binary that leaves the machine, which would ship a language short with nothing saying so. jce_script_enable()'s dist gate (scripting/cmake/JCEScriptEnable.cmake) refuses a JCE_BUILD_VARIANT=dist configure when any language the ENGINE has is missing from the BUILD, unless the caller named LANGUAGES and wrote the omission down. Its first version compared the wrong two sets and could not fail; the negative control caught that, and the version in the tree is the one that fails it: `-DJCE_BUILD_VARIANT=dist -DJCE_BUILD_SCRIPT_VM_PYTHON=OFF` exits 1 naming 'python', a plain dist configure exits 0 with all seven, and release with Python off still exits 0. features.feature: A user project reaches any language model through JCE's own headers
features.evidence: engine/include/jce/middleware/llm/jce_llm.h + api_llm.h. A provider is a PROGRAM: it is handed a prompt file and the path to write its answer to, which is why 'any model' is a claim this can make -- hosted API, local runner, or somebody's shell script around an internal endpoint. The alternative considered and rejected was an HTTP+TLS client in the engine: a new third-party dependency, a certificate store and a per-platform port on a codebase that targets machines from 2008, and it still would not have reached a model behind a script. Single-slot and non-blocking, pumped by jce_llm_tick() once a frame -- the editor pumps it from the FRAME UPDATE and not from the panel's draw, because a hidden panel does not draw and a child whose stdout is never drained blocks in write() and then never exits. Measured in tests/middleware/llm/test_jce_llm.c (12/12), where the test executable is itself the provider so the suite needs no python on PATH: an answer round-trips through the file transport; a non-zero exit, an exit-0 with no file, and an exit-0 with an EMPTY file are each a failure with a message; a child that never exits is killed at the deadline; a previous run's answer cannot be read as this one's; the brief file does not outlive the request; a second submit while one is in flight is refused; and a released handle's number is not reissued. Five mutations -- drop the stale-answer pre-delete, substitute only the first {prompt}, accept an empty answer, remove the deadline, leave the brief on disk -- each kill at least one case.
features.compared: Unity Muse and UE's assistants are hosted, single-vendor, and offer no API a game or tool can call; Godot has no equivalent. Neither exposes a model to a project's own C code at all.

features.feature: Shipped shaders are compiled optimised
features.evidence: OPENED AND CLOSED THE SAME DAY, in that order on purpose. Found while making Reload Shaders reproduce the build byte-for-byte: tools/compile_shaders.cmake invoked shaderc with no -O at all, on every shader and every backend. Passing NO -O is not the same as -O 0 -- shaderc takes a different path, and on HLSL that path keeps debug information: fs_pbr is 416168 bytes with no flag and 203160 with EVERY level from 0 to 3. RECORDED AS 'behind' FIRST, because changing a shader compiler flag is a claim about frame time and the driver recompiles the bytecode anyway, so a size difference is not by itself a performance difference. Then measured, and only then changed. COMPILES: 530 of 530, all five profiles (s_5_0, spirv, GLSL 120, ESSL 300, metal), 0 failed. The 11 failures in the first sweep were MY invocation forcing the PBR varying.def.sc on shaders that have their own -- not the flag. PIXELS: OpenGL is pixel-identical, 0 differing pixels over the viewport. D3D11 differs by at most 1/255 on a handful of pixels with 0 above 2, which is float reassociation. GPU TIME: graveyard at 2x render scale on D3D11 (the 1x scene is CPU-bound at 2.6 ms GPU and could not have shown it), seven INTERLEAVED samples each to cancel drift: 6.01 ms -> 5.50 ms mean, and the spread narrows from 5.0-7.9 to 5.1-5.8. Verified again on the REAL build output after flipping the flag, not just on hand-compiled blobs. ONE TOOL DEFECT FOUND ON THE WAY, and it was blocking the OpenGL half entirely: assert_backend compared the engine's reported name exactly, so 'OpenGL 3.1' never matched 'opengl' and EVERY OpenGL capture was rejected as a bgfx fallback -- making the backend this tree has had the most backend-specific bugs on the one backend no capture could be verified for. Matching is by family now, longest-first so an ES capture cannot be mistaken for a GL one; the fallback it exists to catch still fails.

features.feature: Graph shaders use the same lighting as the rest of the scene
features.evidence: A GRAPH SHADER IS A DIFFERENT MATERIAL, NOT A DIFFERENT RENDERER. The template carried its own lighting -- one directional light, a pow() specular lobe, a flat ambient term -- and said so honestly, but the consequence was that a Shader Graph surface was lit differently from everything beside it: no shadows, no IBL, no fog, no clustered point lights, no area lights, no wetness, no snow, no tone mapping. It now produces the five material values and fs_pbr_main.sh does the lighting -- the SAME file fs_pbr.sc and fs_pbr_fwdplus.sc use, which is how Unity, Unreal and Godot all wire a graph. Three entry points, one lighting model, differing only in what they #define. fs_pbr_body.sh had to become fs_pbr_decl.sh + fs_pbr_main.sh because generated code must read the samplers declared in the first and be visible to main() in the second, and HLSL will not accept a function used before it is defined; the split is PROVEN INERT by compiling fs_pbr, fs_pbr_fwdplus, fs_pbr_toon, fs_pbr_tint and fs_pbr_fade before and after and comparing the blobs byte for byte. MEASURED with both controls, one entity, only its materialPath changing between runs: a graph driving nothing versus a plain material carrying the same five values renders |A-B| = 0.000 max 0.0 -- pixel-identical, so the lighting is the same code. A graph driving emissive instead gives |B-C| mean 20.89 max 165 on the same entity, so the custom program is live and the identity above is not two inert paths agreeing. TWO MORE SINGLE-SOURCE DEFECTS CLOSED ON THE WAY: an unconnected PBR Output socket had two different meanings -- the codegen wrote metallic 0 / roughness 0.5 into the shader while eval_socket wrote 1 / 1 into the .mat.json -- now one table, jce_sg::output_socket_default, read by both; and shaderc's 30 s budget was calibrated for a 100-line shader, so it now reports a compile that legitimately grew by an order of magnitude (measured: dx11 17.3 s, glsl 3.3 s, essl 3.3 s, spirv 0.6 s, metal 0.5 s) as a failure -- raised to 180 s with those numbers recorded beside it. The engine's PBR shader headers now ship in the SDK's shader_include, because a graph material is compiled by the PROJECT and is lit by the engine's shader.

features.feature: Node library available in the visual shader editor
features.evidence: 11 addable node types -> 51, and the gap was never really the count. A graph could not express saturate, a power, a step, a remap, one channel of anything, a dot product, or any procedural pattern -- which is most of what a material does between its inputs and its output. Added: four geometry inputs (world position, world normal, view direction, screen UV), seventeen float operations, three colour operations, Split and Combine and five vector operations, two UV transforms, five procedural patterns (value noise, fractal noise, voronoi, checker, gradient) and two colour utilities. Its sockets are REPLACED, not appended, because nothing correct could have depended on it, and a saved graph that used it now fails the type check loudly rather than meaning something else quietly. VERIFIED BY COMPILING, not by counting. One generated .matgraph.json wires ONE OF EVERY node type into the PBR Output (58 nodes, 80 links -- codegen prunes anything unreachable, so an unconnected pile would have proved nothing), and the editor's own headless authoring hook compiled it: 'compile & bind OK, persisted 5/5 backend variants' -- D3D11, SPIR-V, GLSL 1.20, ESSL 3.00 and Metal. It renders, lit by the same PBR body as the plain sphere beside it. A unit case walks the WHOLE palette and requires a declaration for every output socket of every addable type -- 362 assertions -- because a type in the menu whose snippet emits nothing is the exact shape this feature kept failing in. Verified by breaking one node's snippet and watching it name that node. TWO MECHANISMS the bigger table needed, both replacing a special case rather than adding one: $O (the output ordinal) so Split's four channels are one expression, and per-socket default expressions -- which absorbed the old 'an unconnected vec2 means mat_uv' rule that only worked while every vec2 socket happened to be a UV. NAMED ABSENCES, deliberately not shipped: no Time node (the PBR fragment shader has no time uniform, and a node with no engine behind it is the defect this row is about), no subgraphs, no custom-HLSL node, no vertex stage, no parameter/uniform declaration.
